title: Tutorial
blurb: A tour of the language in one sitting.
text:
# Learn Vyrn

This tutorial takes about an hour. It assumes you have programmed a little
in some language; if you know Python, most of it will look familiar. Every
example is a complete program: save it as a `.vyrn` file and run it with
`vyrn run file.vyrn`. The output shown is what it really prints (a test
runs every example in this page).

Install Vyrn from its repository:

```bash
cargo install --path .
```

## 1. Hello

```vyrn
main:
    name = "Ada"
    year = 1843
    print("Hello, {name}!")
    print("{name} wrote the first program in {year}, {2026 - year} years ago.")
end
```

It prints:

```text
Hello, Ada!
Ada wrote the first program in 1843, 183 years ago.
```

A program starts at `main:`. A block (the body of `main`, a function, an
`if`) is a line ending in `:` and the lines under it, closed by `end`.
Text in `"..."` can include any expression in `{braces}`.

## 2. Lists, maps and loops

```vyrn
main:
    scores = [72, 95, 88]
    scores.append(100)
    print(scores, len(scores), sum(scores) / len(scores))

    ages = {"Ada": 36, "Alan": 41}
    ages["Grace"] = 85
    each name, age in ages.items():
        print("{name} is {age}")
    end

    squares = [n * n each n in 1 to 5]
    print(squares)
end
```

It prints:

```text
[72, 95, 88, 100] 4 88.75
Ada is 36
Alan is 41
Grace is 85
[1, 4, 9, 16, 25]
```

`[...]` is a list and `{...}` a map. `each` walks through anything you can
loop over; `1 to 5` counts from 1 to 5 inclusive (`0 until 5` stops before
5). `[n * n each n in ...]` builds a list in one line.

## 3. Functions, `let` and `var`

```vyrn
create greet(name, excited = false):
    return "Hello, {name}" + ("!" if excited else ".")
end

create area(width: float, height: float) -> float:
    return width * height
end

main:
    print(greet("Ada"), greet("Alan", excited = true))
    print(area(3.0, 4.5))

    let limit = 10      # `let` never changes
    var count = 0       # `var` can
    loop count < limit:
        count += 3
    end
    print(count)
end
```

It prints:

```text
Hello, Ada. Hello, Alan!
13.5
12
```

Parameters can have defaults and be passed by name (`excited = true`).
Types are optional: `area` declares them, so `vyrn check` tells you if a
call passes the wrong kind of value, before the program runs. `let` names a
value that never changes; `var` one that can. Plain `x = 1` works too, as in
Python.

## 4. Choices: `if` and `when`

```vyrn
enum Shape:
    Circle(radius: float)
    Rect(width: float, height: float)
    Empty
end

create area(s: Shape) -> float:
    when s:
        is Shape.Circle(r): return 3.14159 * r * r
        is Shape.Rect(w, h): return w * h
        is Shape.Empty: return 0.0
    end
end

create size(n: int) -> str:
    if n < 10:
        return "small"
    else if n < 100:
        return "medium"
    else:
        return "large"
    end
end

main:
    print(area(Shape.Circle(1.0)), area(Shape.Rect(2.0, 3.0)), area(Shape.Empty))
    print(size(5), size(50), size(500))
end
```

It prints:

```text
3.14159 6.0 0.0
small medium large
```

An `enum` lists the forms a value can take, and `when` handles each one.
Leave a case out and `vyrn check` tells you which:

```text
error: this `when` does not handle `Shape.Empty`
  = help: add `is Shape.Empty: ...` for each, or an `else:` arm
```

## 5. Structs and objects

```vyrn
struct Point:
    x: float
    y: float

    create length(self) -> float:
        return sqrt(self.x * self.x + self.y * self.y)
    end
end

object Counter:
    count: int = 0

    create add(self, n: int):
        self.count += n
    end
end

main:
    var a = Point(3.0, 4.0)
    var b = a            # a struct is a value: b is a copy
    b.x = 0.0
    print(a.x, b.x, a.length())

    let c = Counter()
    let same = c         # a class is shared: same is c
    same.add(5)
    print(c.count)
end
```

It prints:

```text
3.0 0.0 5.0
5
```

A `struct` is a value, like a number: assigning it copies it. An `object` is
shared: two names can refer to the same object. Methods take `self` first.

## 6. Missing values and errors

```vyrn
struct NotFound:
    name: str
end

create find(name: str) -> int?:
    let people = {"Ada": 36, "Alan": 41}
    if name in people: return people[name]
    return none
end

create age_of(name: str) -> int:
    let age = find(name)
    if age == none: fail NotFound(name)
    return age
end

main:
    print(find("Ada"), find("Bob"))
    print(find("Bob") ?? 0)
    attempt:
        print(age_of("Alan"))
        print(age_of("Bob"))
    catch NotFound as e:
        print("no one called", e.name)
    end
end
```

It prints:

```text
36 none
0
41
no one called Bob
```

`int?` means "an int, or `none`". Vyrn will not let you use it as an `int`
until you have checked: after `if age == none: fail ...`, it knows `age` is
an int. `??` gives a default. `fail` stops with an error, and `attempt` /
`catch` handles it; any struct can be an error.

## 7. Doing several things at once

```vyrn
async create fetch(name: str, seconds: float) -> str:
    await sleep(seconds)
    return "{name} done"
end

main:
    # Both start now and wait at the same time.
    let slow = fetch("slow", 0.02)
    let fast = fetch("fast", 0.01)
    print(await join(slow, fast))

    let jobs = channel()
    jobs.send(1)
    jobs.send(2)
    jobs.close()
    async each job in jobs:
        print("job", job)
    end
end
```

It prints:

```text
("slow done", "fast done")
job 1
job 2
```

Calling an `async` function starts it right away; `await` waits for its result.
While one task waits (here, `sleep`), the others run, so the two fetches
above take as long as the slower one, not both together. A `channel` passes
values between tasks, and `async for` reads them as they arrive.

## 8. Everyday tools

Files, text, sorting and data formats need no packages. Functions that take a
function, such as `sorted(..., key = ...)` and `xs.map(f)`, use the arrow form
`(x) => ...`, or `x => ...` for one parameter.

```vyrn
use vyrn.fs
use vyrn.json
use vyrn.re

struct Sale:
    item: str
    price: float
end

main:
    write_text("sales.csv", "pen,1.5\nbook,12.0\npen,1.5\nlamp,30.25\n")
    var sales = []
    using open("sales.csv") as f:
        each line in f:
            let name, price = line.split(",")
            sales.append(Sale(name, float(price)))
        end
    end

    let total = sales.sum_by(s => s.price)
    print("total: {total:,.2f}")
    print("items:", {s.item each s in sales})
    each s in sorted(sales, key = s => s.price, reverse = true)[:2]:
        print("{s.item:<6}{s.price:>8.2f}")
    end
    print(json.dumps({"count": len(sales), "top": max(sales, key = s => s.price).item}))
    print(re.find_all("\\d+", "order 12, then 345"))
    fs.remove("sales.csv")
end
```

```text
total: 45.25
items: {"pen", "book", "lamp"}
lamp     30.25
book     12.00
{"count":4,"top":"lamp"}
["12", "345"]
```

`using open(path) as f:` closes the file at `end`, even after a failure;
`each line in f` reads it line by line. `"{total:,.2f}"` formats a number as
Python's format specs do. `{... each ...}` makes a set, which drops the
repeated `pen`. `vyrn.os`, `vyrn.fs`, `vyrn.path`, `vyrn.time`, `vyrn.random`,
`vyrn.math`, `vyrn.csv`, `vyrn.task` and an HTTP client complete the toolbox;
`docs/stdlib.md` lists everything.

Type `vyrn` with no file to try code line by line:

```console
>>> xs = [3, 1, 2]
>>> xs.map(x => x * 10)
[30, 10, 20]
```

## 9. Tensors and kernels

```vyrn
kernel create leaky(x: f32) -> f32:
    return x if x > 0.0 else 0.1 * x
end

main:
    let w = tensor([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]])
    let x = tensor([[1.0, -1.0]])
    let y = x @ w           # matrix product
    print(y, y.shape)
    print(leaky(y))         # a kernel runs on every element
    print(leaky(-5.0))      # and on plain numbers
end
```

It prints:

```text
tensor([[-2.0, -2.0]]) (1, 2)
tensor([[-0.2, -0.2]])
-0.5
```

`@` is the matrix product. A `kernel` function is written for one number and
runs on every element of a tensor; inside `on gpu[0]:`, Vyrn turns it into
a GPU program (see `docs/nn.md`).

## 10. Projects

```bash
vyrn new hello
```

creates a project: `vyrn.toml`, `main.vyrn`, a module and a test. Files use
each other with `use`:

```vyrn check
use greeting (greet)

main:
    print(greet("world"))
end
```

`use greeting` loads `greeting.vyrn` from the project, and
`use "github.com/someone/module@v1"` fetches a module from any git host,
locked to an exact version in `vyrn.lock`. Then:

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `vyrn run` | runs the project |
| `vyrn test` | runs every `create test_...()` in `tests/` |
| `vyrn check` | finds mistakes without running |
| `vyrn fmt` | formats your code in the one Vyrn style |
| `vyrn build` | makes one file you can copy to any computer and run |

## 11. A web API

```vyrn check
use vyrn.http

struct Todo:
    id: int
    title: str
end

route GET "/todos/{id}" (id: int, todos):
    return todos[id]
end

route POST "/todos" (body: Todo, todos):
    todos[body.id] = body
    return 201, body
end

main:
    http.provide("todos", {1: Todo(1, "learn Vyrn")})
    http.serve(port = 8080)
end
```

Run it and open `http://127.0.0.1:8080/todos/1`. Each `route` turns a URL
into a function call: `{id}` in the path becomes the `id` parameter, the
JSON body of a `POST` becomes a `Todo`, and what the function returns is
sent back as JSON. `vyrn build --target=wasm32-edge` packages the same
program for Vercel or Cloudflare (see `docs/deploy.md`).

## Where next

- `docs/syntax.md`: the whole syntax on one page, compared with Python.
- `docs/stdlib.md`: what is built in, and the standard library.
- `docs/principles.md`: the rules Vyrn is designed by.
- `examples/`: a web API, a game loop, and model inference.

text:
# Vyrn Syntax Guide (v0.4)

Vyrn keeps what makes Python easy to read (header lines ending in `:`,
indentation, slicing, comprehensions, type hints, `a if c else b`) but has its
own vocabulary: `create`, `each`, `loop`, `when`, `using`, `attempt`, `object`.
Each word says what the line does, so Vyrn code is recognisably Vyrn. Every block closes with `end`,
so pasted or reformatted code cannot silently change meaning.

The formal definition is [`grammar.ebnf`](grammar.ebnf).

## Five rules

1. **A header ends with `:`.** After it comes either one statement on the
   same line, or a block closed by `end`.

   ```vyrn
   if lives == 0: stop

   each enemy in enemies:
       enemy.update(dt)
   end
   ```

2. **A chain shares one `end`.** `else if`, `else`, `is`, `catch` and `always`
   continue the statement above them.

   ```vyrn
   if score >= 90:
       grade = "A"
   else if score >= 80: grade = "B"
   else: grade = "F"
   end
   ```

   A one-line `if` cannot take an `else if` or `else`. Use the block form, or
   the expression `grade = "A" if score >= 90 else "F"`.

3. **Programs start at `main:`.** The top level of a file holds declarations
   only; statements run inside `main` or a function.

4. **Assignment declares, as in Python.** `total = 0` creates a variable.
   `let` makes a name fixed, `var` declares one explicitly, and `const` is
   computed at compile time. Inside `strict` and `kernel` functions every new
   name needs `let`, `var` or `const`, so a typo cannot create a variable.

5. **Everything past the name is optional.** Types, ownership, lifetime and
   hardware are added only when you need them:

   ```vyrn
   weights = load("model.bin")
   let weights: tensor[f16; V, D] = load("model.bin")
   let weights: tensor[f16; V, D] on gpu[0] = load("model.bin")
   let weights: shared tensor[f16; V, D] on gpu[0 to 3] = load("model.bin")
   ```

## Python to Vyrn

### Same as Python

`if` `else` `and` `or` `not` `in` `not in` `return` `async` `await` `self`
`@decorator` `x: int` `-> int`
`a if c else b` `x[1:9:2]` `x[:, -1]` `x[..., none]` `+ - * / // % **`
`== != < <= > >=` `"""multi-line"""` `'single'` `"double"` `r"raw"` `#` comments

### Vyrn's own words

| Python | Vyrn | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `def f(x):` | `create f(x):` ... `end` | Says what the line does: it creates a function |
| `elif c:` | `else if c:` | Two plain words, as in most languages |
| `for x in xs:` | `each x in xs:` | Says what happens: once for each item |
| `while c:` | `loop c:` | One word for every loop; `loop:` alone runs forever |
| `match x:` / `case P:` | `when x:` / `is P:` | Reads as a sentence: `when x:` / `is 0:` |
| `with open(p) as f:` | `using open(p) as f:` | Says the resource is in use until `end` |
| `try: ... finally: f()` (or Go's `defer`) | `defer f()`, `defer x -= 1` | Runs a statement when the block ends, however it ends; several run last first |
| `try:` / `finally:` | `attempt:` / `always:` | `always` runs whether or not something failed |
| `class Point:` | `object Point:` | Says what it makes |
| `[x * 2 for x in xs]` | `[x * 2 each x in xs]` | Comprehensions read like loops |
| `sum(x * x for x in xs)` | `sum(x * x each x in xs)` | A generator: items worked out one at a time, as they are asked for; `(x each x in xs)` on its own |
| `lambda x: x * 2` | `(x) => x * 2` or `x => x * 2` | No keyword: the arrow says it all |
| `Callable[[int], str]` | `(int) -> str` | A function type looks like a function |
| `f"Hi {name}"` | `"Hi {name}"` | Every string interpolates; no prefix to forget |
| `True` `False` `None` | `true` `false` `none` | Lowercase like every other keyword |
| `break` / `continue` | `stop` / `skip` | Plain English |
| `pass` | (nothing) | `end` closes an empty block |
| `import x` / `from x import a` | `use x` / `use x (a)` | One form for both |
| `raise E` | `fail E` | Pairs with `fails E` in signatures |
| `except E as e:` | `catch E as e:` | The common word across languages |
| `range(0, 10)` | `0 until 10` | `0 to 10` includes 10; `by 2` sets the step |
| `if __name__ == "__main__":` | `main:` | One obvious entry point |
| `x.T` | `x.T` | Unchanged: transpose is a property, as in PyTorch |

Writing a Python word out of habit is not a mystery error: the parser names
the Vyrn word, as in "`while` is not a Vyrn keyword" with the hint "write
`loop condition:`". The retired words (`while`, `match`, `class`, ...) are
ordinary names in Vyrn, so `match = find(xs)` is fine. `create` is a
keyword only where it declares a function (`create greet(name):`), so
`create(x)` and `db.create(row)` are ordinary calls.

### Added for 2026-era code

| Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `let` / `var` / `const` | Fixed, mutable, compile-time names |
| `struct` | Value type with a fixed layout (stored as columns in arrays) |
| `enum`, `trait`, `impl` | Tagged unions, interfaces, implementations |
| `x?.name`, `x ?? default` | Optional chaining and default for `none` |
| `xs \|> sum` | Pipeline |
| `-> T fails E` | Typed errors; a failure passes up to the caller until a `catch` |
| `mut x`, `own x` | Mutable borrow, ownership transfer (no lifetimes) |
| `a @ b`, `a * b` | Matrix product, element-wise product |
| `tensor[f16; B, T, D]` | Tensor type with checked shape |
| `on gpu[0]:`, `x on cpu` | Run or place on a device |
| `region frame:`, `on frame` | Memory arena freed in one step |
| `route GET "/users/{id}" (id: u64):` | HTTP route, implicitly async |
| `spawn task`, `par each` | Concurrent task, parallel loop |
| `strict create`, `kernel create` | Fully typed function, GPU/SIMD function |

## The four examples

- [`examples/grade.vyrn`](../examples/grade.vyrn): beginner, no types at all
- [`examples/game.vyrn`](../examples/game.vyrn): game loop with fixed-size data and a frame region
- [`examples/api.vyrn`](../examples/api.vyrn): async JSON routes
- [`examples/inference.vyrn`](../examples/inference.vyrn): tensor layers spread across GPUs

# The Vyrn Standard Library

Status: v0.4. Where an API already runs in the interpreter it
says **runs today**; everything else is design, which this document fixes so
that implementation can follow it. Syntax follows `docs/grammar.ebnf` v0.4.

## 1. Three tiers

| Tier | How you get it | What belongs there |
|---|---|---|
| **Prelude** | Always in scope, no `use` | What a beginner needs in their first hour: core types, `print`, `len`, `open`, collections, tensor math |
| **`vyrn.*` modules** | `use vyrn.http`, `use vyrn.fs`, ... | Capabilities with a larger surface, a lifecycle or I/O policy: servers, memory mapping, task supervision, neural-network layers |
| **Packages** | `use app.storage (Db)` | Everything else, versioned by the package manager |

A name earns a place in the Prelude only if all four hold:

1. **Beginner-first.** A first script would otherwise need a `use` line for it.
2. **Free when unused.** It is a builtin in the VM's table or a type the
   compiler knows. Nothing is initialized or linked until a program calls it.
3. **No policy.** It takes no position on how to structure an application.
   `print` and `open` qualify. A router, a thread pool or a logging framework
   does not.
4. **Stable.** It will not need a breaking change. APIs still evolving live in
   a module, where a new version can sit beside the old one.

### Name resolution

Names resolve innermost first, so a program can always shadow the Prelude:

1. locals and parameters (innermost block first), then captured variables
2. top-level declarations of the file
3. names brought in by `use ... (a, b as c)`
4. the Prelude

`use vyrn.http` binds the module to the name `http` and nothing else. There
are no glob imports, so reading a file tells you where every name comes
from. `use vyrn.http as web` renames the module. **Runs today:** this order is
what `src/vm/compiler.rs` (`resolve`) implements, and `use vyrn.web` /
`use vyrn.http` with both import forms works.

## 2. The Prelude

### 2.1 Types

The Prelude's types are the language's own. The familiar long names map to
Vyrn's spelling as follows:

| Concept | Vyrn spelling | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| String | `str` | UTF-8, immutable, shared by reference count; slicing makes a view |
| List | `[T]` | Growable, shared by reference; `[T; N]` is a fixed array stored inline |
| Map | `{K: V}` | Insertion-ordered hash map |
| Tensor | `tensor[dtype; dims]` | `tensor[f32]` leaves the rank open; `vec2`/`vec3`/`vec4` are small tensors |
| Optional | `T?` | `none` or a `T`; `x?.f` and `x ?? default` |
| Numbers | `int` (`i8` to `u64`), `float` (`f16`, `bf16`, `f32`, `f64`), `bool` | |
| Tuples | `(A, B)` | `()` is the unit type |
| Tasks | `Task[T]`, `Channel[T]` | What an `async` function call and `channel()` return |
| Errors | `Error` and the built-in kinds (`IoError`, `KeyError`, `TypeError`, `NotFound`, ...) | Any struct can be passed to `fail` |

### 2.2 Functions

| Group | Names | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Input and output | `print`, `input(prompt)` | runs today |
| Conversion | `str`, `int` (`int("ff", 16)` reads other bases), `float`, `bool`, `list`, `dict`, `set`, `repr`, `chr`, `ord`, `hex`, `oct`, `bin`, `typeof` | runs today |
| Sequences | `len`, `range`, `enumerate`, `zip`, `reversed`, `any`, `all`, `sum`, and `sorted`, `min`, `max` with `key =` (and `reverse =` for `sorted`), `map(f, xs)`, `filter(f, xs)` | runs today |
| Math | `abs`, `round`, `sqrt`, `exp`, `tanh`, `floor`, `ceil`, `pow`, `divmod` | runs today |
| Text | `format(value, spec)`; the same specs inside strings: `"{price:.2f}"`, `"{n:,}"`, `"{name:>8}"`, `"{ratio:.1%}"`, `"{n:#x}"` | runs today |
| Files | `open(path, mode = "r")` returning a `File` (`read`, `readline`, `lines`, `write`, `write_line`, `close`; `each line in f`) for use with `using`; `read_text`, `write_text` | runs today |
| Data | `parse_json`, `to_json` | runs today |
| Tasks | `sleep`, `channel`, `join`, `now` | runs today |
| Games | `Clock(hz, frames)` | runs today |
| Tensors | `tensor`, `zeros`, `ones`, `rand`, `arange`, `eye`, `vec2`/`vec3`/`vec4`, `softmax`, `relu`, `gelu`, `argmax`, `@`, `memory`, `fit`, `set_memory_limit`, `format_bytes` | runs today |
| Weights | `load_weights`, `save_weights`, `load_tokenizer` | runs today; moving to `vyrn.nn` (section 6) |
| Devices | `cpu`, `gpu` (indexed: `gpu[0]`, `gpu[0 to 3]`) | runs today |

`open` belongs in the Prelude because reading a file is part of a first
script, and `using` already makes it safe:

```vyrn
using open("scores.txt") as f:
    each line in f.lines():
        print(line)
    end
end
```

`using` calls `close()` on every way out of the block, including failures
(**runs today**). `"w"` replaces a file and `"a"` adds to its end.

### 2.3 Methods of strings, lists, maps and sets

All **run today**. Methods that take a function (`map`, `filter`, `sort`
with `key =`, ...) are written in Vyrn itself, in `src/prelude.vyrn`.

| Type | Methods |
|---|---|
| `str` | `upper`, `lower`, `title`, `capitalize`, `swapcase`, `strip`/`lstrip`/`rstrip` (optionally of given characters), `split(sep, limit)`, `rsplit`, `lines`, `chars`, `join`, `replace`, `startswith`, `endswith`, `find`, `rfind`, `index`, `count`, `contains`, `partition`, `rpartition`, `removeprefix`, `removesuffix`, `zfill`, `ljust`, `rjust`, `center`, `repeat`, `format(spec)`, `isdigit`, `isalpha`, `isalnum`, `isspace`, `isupper`, `islower`, `is_empty`, `encode` |
| `[T]` | `append`, `extend`, `insert`, `pop`, `remove`, `clear`, `sort(key, reverse)`, `reverse`, `copy`, `index`, `count`, `contains`, `first`, `last`, `is_empty`, `unique`, `join(sep)`, `chunks(n)`, `sum`; taking a function: `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `find`, `find_index`, `any`, `all`, `count_if`, `min_by`, `max_by`, `sum_by`, `group_by`, `each`, `take_while`, `drop_while`; and `flatten` |
| `{K: V}` | `keys`, `values`, `items`, `get(key, default)`, `pop(key, default)`, `update`, `setdefault`, `has`, `copy`, `clear`, `is_empty`; taking a function: `map_values`, `filter` |
| set | `{1, 2, 3}`, `{x each x in xs}` or `set(xs)`; `add`, `remove`, `discard`, `has`, `union`, `intersection`, `difference`, `symmetric_difference`, `issubset`, `issuperset`, `copy`, `clear`; the operators `|`, `&`, `-`, `^`; `in`; `len` |

A program may declare its own `map`, `sorted` or any other Prelude name;
its declaration wins.

## 3. `vyrn.http`: a FastAPI-style async router

`vyrn.http` turns the language's `route` declarations into a running server.
The design follows FastAPI's three ideas, adapted to a compiled language:

1. **The signature is the contract.** Parameters are filled from the path,
   then the query string, then the request body, then registered providers.
   Declared types are checked before the handler runs (a `400` otherwise),
   and the declared result type is the response schema.
2. **Dependency injection by name and type.** `http.provide("db", db)` makes
   every route parameter named `db` receive that value. Tests provide fakes
   the same way.
3. **Every handler is a task.** A route body is implicitly `async`; awaiting
   a database or a model never blocks other requests.

```vyrn
use vyrn.http

struct Item:
    id: int
    name: str
end

struct NotFound:
    id: int
end

route GET "/items/{id}" (id: int, db) -> Item fails NotFound:
    if id not in db: fail NotFound(id)
    return db[id]
end

route POST "/items" (body: Item, db) -> (int, Item):
    db[body.id] = body
    return 201, body
end

main:
    http.provide("db", {1: Item(1, "lamp")})
    http.serve(port = 8080)
end
```

**Runs today:** `route` and `routes` groups, path parameters converted to
their declared types, query parameters, a JSON `body` converted to the
declared struct (a missing field is a `400`), `http.provide`,
`http.serve(port, host, requests)`, handlers running as concurrent tasks,
and responses built from return values. A string is sent as `text/plain`,
`(status, value)` sets the status, `none` is `204`, anything else is JSON.
A failure is a JSON error whose status follows its kind: `NotFound` is 404,
`BadRequest` 400, `Unauthorized` 401, `Forbidden` 403, otherwise 500.
`vyrn.web` is the same module under its earlier name.

### 3.1 Requests, responses, middleware, live connections

**Runs today.** Three parameter names are special: a route that takes
`request` gets the whole request, one that takes `stream` sends
server-sent events, and one that takes `socket` is a WebSocket.

| API | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `request` parameter | `request.method`, `path`, `headers` (names in lower case), `query`, `cookies`, `form` (the fields of a submitted HTML form), `body` (text), `json` (the body parsed, or none), `client`, and `request.header("X-Key")` in any case. Form fields also fill route parameters by name, as query parameters do |
| `http.cookie(name, value, max_age, path, http_only = true, secure, same_site = "Lax")` | The text of a `Set-Cookie` header: `http.Response(303, "", {"Set-Cookie": http.cookie("session", id), "Location": "/"})`; `max_age = 0` deletes it |
| `http.Response(status, body, headers)` | Full control: `return http.Response(201, item, {"Location": "/items/7"})`. A `Content-Type` header replaces the usual one |
| `http.use(f)` | Middleware around every route: `f(request, next)` gives the response, usually `next(request)`'s, or answers by itself (a 401, a cached page). The first added runs outermost |
| `stream` parameter | Server-sent events: `stream.send(data, event = "name")` pushes one to the page (text as it is, anything else as JSON); the stream ends with the handler. Pages listen with `new EventSource("/path")` |
| `socket` parameter | A WebSocket: `socket.send(x)`, `msg = await socket.receive()` (JSON arrives as maps and lists, other text as text; none once the other side closes), `socket.close()`, `socket.closed` |
| `http.get`, `http.post`, ... | Calling other services (see 5a) |
| `http.test(method, path, body, headers, form)` | Sends a request to the program's own routes, through its middleware, without a network: `http.test("POST", "/signup", form = {"name": "Ada"})`. Gives a response like `http.get`'s. For tests and trying routes out |

```vyrn check
use vyrn.http

create needs_key(request, next):
    if request.header("X-Key") != "secret": return http.Response(401, {"error": "no key"})
    return next(request)
end

route GET "/clock" (stream):
    each i in 1 to 10:
        stream.send({"tick": i})
        await sleep(1)
    end
end

route GET "/chat" (socket):
    socket.send("welcome")
    loop:
        let msg = await socket.receive()
        if msg == none: stop
        socket.send("you said: {msg}")
    end
end

main:
    http.use(needs_key)
    http.serve(port = 8080)
end
```

Still design: `http.Router(prefix)` values for mounting modules (the
`routes "/prefix":` group covers most of it today), and
`http.serve(workers = n)` with a listener per OS thread.

What stays out: templates, ORMs, sessions. Those are packages.

## 4. `vyrn.fs`: files, and memory mapping without copies

The Prelude's `open` covers reading and writing. `vyrn.fs` is for programs
where copies matter: model weights, datasets, logs larger than RAM.

```vyrn
use vyrn.fs

create count_errors(path: str) -> int:
    var errors = 0
    using fs.map(path) as data:
        each line in data.lines():
            if line.startswith("ERROR"): errors += 1
        end
    end
    return errors
end
```

`fs.map(path)` maps the file into the address space (`mmap`, or
`MapViewOfFile` on Windows) and returns a `Mapped` value. No byte is read
until it is touched, and nothing is copied:

- `len(data)` and `data.size` are its length in bytes; `data.text(start, end)`
  and `data.bytes(start, end)` read a range; `data.find(text, start)` gives
  where some text first appears (or -1); `data.count_lines()` counts lines
  without making them; `data.lines()` gives every line as text.
- `fs.tensor_view(data, dtype, shape, offset)` makes a tensor from `f32`,
  `f16` or `bf16` values at a byte offset, such as one weight out of a
  model file.

Only the pages a program touches are read from disk. What it reads out
(text, numbers, a tensor) is copied into Vyrn values; zero-copy views that
the borrow checker keeps inside the `using` block are the next step.

**Why this matters for large models.** A 14B-parameter model at 4 bits is
about 8 GB on disk. Reading it into a buffer and then uploading it costs
8 GB of RAM on top of the GPU copy. Mapping it means the pages stream from
the page cache straight into the GPU upload (`vyrn.nn` uses this, section 6),
and on a 32 GB machine nothing is held twice.

**Runs today:** `fs.exists`, `fs.is_file`, `fs.is_dir`, `fs.list(dir)`,
`fs.walk(dir)`, `fs.mkdir` (with parents), `fs.remove` (files and
directories), `fs.rename`, `fs.copy`, `fs.size`, `fs.modified`,
`fs.read_text`, `fs.write_text`, `fs.append_text`, `fs.read_lines`. A file
that is not there fails with `NotFound`. `fs.map` and `fs.tensor_view`, as
above. Still design:

| API | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `fs.map_mut(path, size) -> MappedMut` | Writable mapping; changes reach the file on `flush()` or at the end of `using` |
| `fs.glob(pattern)`, `fs.stat(path)` | Directory work beyond `fs.walk` |
| `fs.watch(path)` | A `Channel` of change events, for `async for` |

On WebAssembly there is no `mmap`, so `fs.map` reads the file into linear
memory once. Programs keep the same code and lose only the laziness.

## 5. `vyrn.task`: green threads and supervision

**Runs today, in the language itself:** every `async` function call starts a
*green thread*. Tasks are stackful, so any function can `await`, and each
suspended task costs only its own registers and frames. A single-threaded
scheduler runs them with timers and channels, reports deadlocks, and warns
about failed tasks nobody awaited. The Prelude keeps the everyday part:
`spawn`, `await`, `async for`, `sleep`, `channel`, `join`.

`vyrn.task` adds the structure that larger programs need.

```vyrn
use vyrn.task

async create fetch(url: str) -> str:
    await sleep(0.1)
    return "page at {url}"
end

async create crawl(urls: [str]) -> [str]:
    # Structured concurrency: the group outlives none of its tasks. Tasks
    # still running at `end` are cancelled.
    using task.group() as g:
        each url in urls: g.spawn(fetch(url))
        return await g.wait()
    end
end
```

**Runs today:** everything below. Awaiting a cancelled task fails with
`Cancelled`.

| API | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `task.group()` | Structured concurrency, as above: `g.spawn(work)`, `await g.wait()` (or `await g`) for every result, `g.cancel()` to stop the unfinished |
| `task.timeout(seconds, work)` | `await task.timeout(2.0, fetch(url))` gives the result, or fails with `Timeout` and stops the work |
| `task.parallel(work, items, workers)` | `[work(x) each x in items]` spread over every CPU core: each worker thread runs its own copy of the program, so nothing is shared and nothing needs locking. `work` is a top-level function; items and results are plain data (numbers, text, lists, maps, sets, structs) |
| `task.select(a, b, ...)` | Waits for the first of several tasks or channels; `await` gives `(index, value)` |
| `task.cancel(t)`, `task.done(t)` | Stop a task; whether it has finished |
| `task.yield_now()` | Lets other tasks run inside a long computation |
| `channel(capacity = n)` | A bounded channel: `ch.send(x)` waits while it is full, which slows a fast producer to its consumer's pace; `ch.capacity()`, `ch.full()`, `ch.len()` |
| `task.Pool(workers = n)` | Threads that stay ready for CPU-heavy calls: `await pool.run(f, args...)` runs `f` on one of them while other tasks keep running, `await pool.map(f, items)` spreads the items over them, `pool.close()` stops them. As with `task.parallel`, `f` is a top-level function and values are copied between threads, so nothing is shared; a failure there comes back as `PoolError` |

The split follows the cost model. Green threads are cheap and share one OS
thread, so the Prelude has them. A `Pool` adds threads, and with them the
rule that values cross threads only by `own`. That is an explicit choice,
so it sits behind `use vyrn.task`.

### Testing with fakes

`vyrn test` runs every `create test_...()` in `tests/`; `assert(condition,
message)` checks, and a failed comparison says both sides
(`AssertionError: 6 == 5 is false`). `assert_fails(() => f(x), "ValueError")`
checks that a call fails (with that kind, if given) and gives the error. To test code without its real dependencies (a database,
the network, the clock), pass it a **fake**:

| API | Does |
|---|---|
| `fake(returns = x)` | A stand-in function that gives back `x` |
| `fake(returns_each = [a, b])`, `fake(fails = ValueError("..."))` | One value per call; or failing on purpose |
| `fake(methods = {"save": fake(returns = true)})` | A stand-in object; any other method is a fake too |
| `f.calls`, `f.call_count`, `f.called`, `f.last_call`, `f.called_with(args...)`, `f.reset()` | What happened to it |

### `vyrn.db`: SQLite databases

```vyrn
use vyrn.db

main:
    using db.open("shop.db") as conn:
        conn.execute("create table if not exists items (name text, price real)")
        conn.execute("insert into items values (?, ?)", ["pen", 1.5])
        each row in conn.query("select * from items where price < ?", [10]):
            print(row["name"], row["price"])
        end
    end
end
```

|---|---|
| `db.open(path)` | A database file (made if missing); `":memory:"` lives only while the program runs |
| `conn.execute(sql, params)` | Runs a statement, gives the rows changed; several statements without params run as a script |
| `conn.execute_many(sql, rows)` | One statement per row of params |
| `conn.query(sql, params)` | Every row, as maps from column to value |
| `conn.query_one(...)`, `conn.value(...)` | The first row, or its first column; `none` when there is none |
| `conn.last_id()`, `conn.tables()` | The last inserted row id; the table names |
| `conn.begin()`, `conn.commit()`, `conn.rollback()`, `conn.close()` | Transactions; `using` closes |
| `conn.create_table(name, columns)` | A table from `{"name": "text", "age": "int"}`, plus an `id` column |
| `conn.insert(table, record)` | Adds a map or struct as a row; gives its `id` |

| `conn.update(table, where, changes)`, `conn.delete(table, where)` | How many rows changed; `delete` needs a `where` |

from the SQL, so input cannot change a statement. Errors are
`DatabaseError` with SQLite's message.

| `world.raycast(origin, direction, max = 100, ignore = body)` | The first body along a line: `body`, `point`, `normal`, `distance`, or none |
| `world.collisions()`, `world.remove(body)`, `world.bodies` | Pairs that started touching in the last step; removing bodies |

`examples/physics.vyrn` is a room of crates to walk around and knock over.

### `vyrn.html`: reading web pages

`html.parse(text)` gives a page; `page.select(css)` and
`page.select_one(css)` find elements by CSS selector (`"a[href]"`,
`"div.price"`, `"#main > p"`). An element has `text`, `raw_text`, `tag`,
`html`, `outer_html`, `id`, `classes`, `attrs`, `children`, `parent`,
`attr(name)`, `has_class(name)` and its own `select`. `page.title`,
`page.text`. `html.escape(text)` makes text safe for a page (`<` to
`<`), and `html.unescape(text)` turns entities back (`"` to `"`,
`'` to `'`). Pages are read as browsers read them.

### `vyrn.template`: pages made from data

```vyrn
use vyrn.template

main:
    let page = template.render(r"<h1>{{title}}</h1>{{#each items}}<li>{{name}}</li>{{/each}}",
                               {"title": "Shop", "items": [{"name": "pen"}]})
    print(page)
end
```

`{{name}}` (HTML-escaped), `{{{raw}}}`, `{{a.b}}` (map keys and struct
fields), `{{#each list}}` with `{{this}}` and `{{@index}}` (and `{{else}}` for an empty list), `{{#if x}}` /
`{{else}}` / `{{/if}}`, `{{#unless x}}`, `{{! comment }}`.
`template.render_file(path, data)` reads the template from a file. Write
templates in raw strings `r"..."` or files: in ordinary strings `{...}`
interpolates. A route returning text that starts with `<` is sent as a web
page.

### `vyrn.table`: data in rows and columns

| API | Does |
|---|---|
| `table.read_csv(path)`, `table.from_csv(text)`, `table.from_rows(rows, columns)` | A table; numbers in CSV become numbers, empty cells `none` |
| `t.head(n)`, `t.tail(n)`, `t.row(i)`, `t.column(name)`, `t.columns`, `t.rows`, `t.shape`, `len(t)` | Looking at it; `print(t)` shows an aligned table |
| `t.where(column, op, value)` | Rows that match: `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `contains`, `startswith`, `in` |
| `t.sort(column, descending)`, `t.select(columns)`, `t.add_column(name, values)` | New tables |
| `t.sum`, `t.mean`, `t.median`, `t.min`, `t.max`, `t.count`, `t.unique` | Of one column |
| `t.group_by(column, value, how)` | One row per group: `how` is sum, mean, median, min, max or count |
| `t.keep(mask)` | The rows where a list of true/false says true: `t.keep([r["age"] > 30 each r in t])` |
| `t.drop_missing(columns)`, `t.fill_missing(column, value)` | Without rows that have empty cells (in those columns, or any); with empty cells filled |
| `t.rename(old, new)`, `t.drop(column)` | New tables with a column renamed or removed |
| `t.join(other, on, how = "inner")` | Each row with the other table's matching rows beside it; `how = "left"` keeps rows with no match |
| `t.describe()` | A table of count, mean, min and max for each number column |
| `t.to_csv(path)`, `each row in t` | Writing, and rows as maps |

### `vyrn.chart`: charts

`chart.line(xs, ys)`, `chart.scatter(xs, ys)`, `chart.bar(labels,
values)`, `chart.hist(values, bins)`, `chart.pie(labels, values)`, each with
`title`, `x_label`, `y_label`, `width`, `height`. A map of name to values
draws several series with a legend. `c.save("chart.png")` or
`c.save("chart.svg")`; `c.svg()` gives the SVG text.

### `vyrn.crypto`: hashing, passwords and tokens

| API | Does |
|---|---|
| `crypto.hash_password(pw)` | Text safe to store instead of a password: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, 100,000 rounds, a random salt (`pbkdf2-sha256$rounds$salt$hash`) |
| `crypto.check_password(pw, stored)` | Whether `pw` is the password `stored` was made from |
| `crypto.token(bytes = 32)` | A secure random token in hex, for session ids, reset links and API keys |
| `crypto.sha256(text)`, `crypto.hmac(key, text)` | A hash; a signature only the key's holder can make (hex) |
| `crypto.same(a, b)` | Equality in constant time, for comparing tokens and signatures |

### `vyrn.mail`: sending email

`mail.send(to, subject, body, sender, server, port, user, password,
security, html)`: `to` is an address or a list; `security` is
`"starttls"` (port 587, the default), `"tls"` (465) or `"none"`. Keep
passwords out of code: `password = os.env("MAIL_PASSWORD")`.

## 6. Tensors: the Prelude and `vyrn.nn`

The line is **math versus models**.

**Prelude: tensor math.** The tensor type, constructors, element-wise
arithmetic, `@`, reductions and the standard element-wise functions
(`exp`, `tanh`, `relu`, `gelu`, `softmax`) are numeric primitives in the
same sense as `+` on integers. They compile to the VM's tensor instructions
(`MatMul`, `Place`, ...), which a `TensorBackend` executes per device. That
is the CPU reference or the wgpu GPU backend (**runs today**,
`cargo build --features gpu`). They have no state and no configuration, so
`x @ w` means the same thing in every program. Placement is part of the
language (`on gpu[0]:`, `x on gpu[1]`), not of a library.

**`vyrn.nn`: model building blocks.** Layers carry parameters and state,
model formats change, and sampling strategies are a matter of taste. These
need versioning, so they live in a module:

**Runs today:**

| API | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `nn.load(path, dtype = "q4")` | The tensors of a safetensors file as a map of name to tensor, read one at a time (never the whole file twice) and converted on the way if asked; `fit` then spreads them over devices |
| `nn.save(path, tensors)` | Writes a map of name to tensor |
| `nn.tokenizer(path)` | A Hugging Face `tokenizer.json`: `tok.encode(text)`, `tok.decode(ids)` |
| `nn.sample(logits, temperature = 1, top_k = 0, top_p = 1)` | The next token from logits (a list, or a tensor's last row). Temperature 0 picks the likeliest; `random.seed` makes runs repeat |
| `nn.generate(step, tokens, max_new = 50, temperature, top_k, top_p, stop_at)` | A generator of new tokens: your `step(tokens)` runs the model and gives the logits, so any architecture written in Vyrn works. `each t in nn.generate(...)` streams them |

```vyrn
use vyrn.nn

create reply(model, tok, prompt: str) -> str:
    create step(tokens: list): return model.forward(tokens)
    var out = []
    each t in nn.generate(step, tok.encode(prompt), max_new = 100, temperature = 0.7, top_p = 0.9):
        out.append(t)
    end
    return tok.decode(out)
end
```

**Design, next:**

| API | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `nn.Linear`, `nn.Embedding`, `nn.RMSNorm`, `nn.Attention`, `nn.MLP` | Layers as structs: weights are fields, `forward` is a `kernel` function |
| `nn.KVCache(layers, max_tokens)` | Preallocated attention cache, placed with the layers |

`load_weights`, `save_weights` and `load_tokenizer` remain in the Prelude
as other names for `nn.load`, `nn.save` and `nn.tokenizer`.

## 7. Two complete programs

### 7.1 A first script: no `use` at all

Everything here is Prelude: types, `open`, `using`, string methods, lists,
maps, tensors.

```vyrn
# grades.vyrn: read "name,score" lines and summarize them.

main:
    scores = {}
    using open("grades.csv") as f:
        each line in f.lines():
            let parts = line.split(",")
            scores[parts[0]] = float(parts[1])
        end
    end

    let values = tensor(scores.values())
    print("students: {len(scores)}")
    print("average:  {round(values.sum() / len(scores), 1)}")

    each name, score in scores.items():
        let grade = "A" if score >= 90 else "B" if score >= 80 else "C"
        print("{name}: {score} ({grade})")
    end
end
```

### 7.2 An inference server: explicit dependencies

The `use` lines name exactly what the program depends on beyond the
Prelude. The model is memory-mapped and spread across GPUs, each request is
a task, and generation streams over server-sent events.

```vyrn
use vyrn.http
use vyrn.fs
use vyrn.task
use vyrn.nn
use app.auth (require_key)

struct Prompt:
    text: str
    max_tokens: int = 128
end

struct Health:
    model: str
    gpu_memory: str
end

const MODEL = "models/sml-14b-q4.safetensors"

route GET "/health" (model) -> Health:
    return Health(MODEL, format_bytes(memory_used(gpu[0])))
end

routes "/v1":
    @require_key
    route POST "/complete" (body: Prompt, model, tokenizer) -> str:
        let tokens = tokenizer.encode(body.text)
        let output = await task.timeout(30.0, model.complete(tokens, body.max_tokens))
        return tokenizer.decode(output)
    end

    @require_key
    route SSE "/stream" (body: Prompt, model, tokenizer, stream):
        let tokens = tokenizer.encode(body.text)
        async each token in nn.generate(model, tokens, body.max_tokens):
            await stream.send(tokenizer.decode([token]))
        end
    end
end

main:
    # Pages stream from disk to the GPUs; nothing is held twice in RAM.
    let model = nn.load(MODEL, dtype = "q4", devices = gpu[0 to 1])
    http.provide("model", model)
    http.provide("tokenizer", nn.Tokenizer.load("models/tokenizer.json"))
    http.serve(port = 8080)
end
```

## 8. Implementation status

| Piece | Where | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Prelude functions and types | `src/vm/builtins.rs`, `src/vm/stdlib.rs`, `src/prelude.vyrn` | runs |
| Files, sets, format specs, methods (section 2) | `src/vm/stdlib.rs`, `src/vm/builtins.rs` | runs |
| `vyrn.os`, `vyrn.path`, `vyrn.time`, `vyrn.random`, `vyrn.math`, `vyrn.json`, `vyrn.re`, `vyrn.csv`, HTTP client | `src/vm/stdlib.rs` | runs |
| `vyrn.db`, `vyrn.draw`, `vyrn.html`, `vyrn.template`, `vyrn.table`, `vyrn.chart`, `vyrn.mail` | `src/vm/lib_*.rs` | runs |
| `use vyrn.<module>` with module and name imports | `src/vm/compiler.rs` (`use_decl`, `module_member`) | runs |
| `vyrn.http` routing, providers, server, requests, responses, middleware, SSE, WebSockets | `src/vm/machine.rs` (`resolve_route`, `service_servers`), `src/vm/web.rs`, `src/vm/web_live.rs` | runs; `Router` values and multi-threaded serving are design |
| Green threads, channels, timers | `src/vm/machine.rs`, `src/vm/task.rs` | runs |
| `vyrn.task` groups, timeouts, select, cancel, pools, bounded channels, `yield_now` | `src/vm/stdlib.rs`, `src/vm/parallel.rs`, `src/vm/machine.rs` (`await_race`, `apply_cancels`) | runs |
| `vyrn.fs` files and directories | `src/vm/stdlib.rs` | runs |
| `vyrn.fs` mapping (`fs.map`, `fs.tensor_view`) | `src/vm/lib_nn.rs` | runs; zero-copy views depend on borrow checking of slices (`src/check.rs`) |
| Tensor math on CPU and GPU | `src/vm/tensor.rs`, `src/vm/gpu.rs` | runs |
| `vyrn.nn` load, save, tokenizer, sample, generate | `src/vm/weights.rs`, `src/vm/tokenizer.rs`, `src/vm/lib_nn.rs`, `src/prelude.vyrn` (`__nn_generate`) | runs; layer structs and `KVCache` are design |

Build order from here: zero-copy views of mapped files (borrowed slices),
then `vyrn.nn` layer structs and the `KVCache`, then `http.Router` values
and multi-threaded serving.

title: Packages
text:
# Packages

A Vyrn package is a git repository with `.vyrn` files. Using one is a
`use` line; finding one is the registry.

## Using a package

```bash
vyrn search physics
```

```bash
vyrn add physics-extra
```

`vyrn add` finds the package in the registry, fetches its newest release,
and pins it in `vyrn.lock`. It prints the `use` line to write:

```vyrn
use "github.com/ann/physics-extra@v1"
```

`@v1` means "the newest v1.x.y", so fixes arrive with `vyrn add` again
without breaking changes; `@v1.4.2` pins one exact release. Packages that
are not in the registry are added by URL the same way:
`vyrn add github.com/ann/neural@v1`.

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `vyrn search [words]` | packages whose name, keywords or description have every word |
| `vyrn info <name>` | its versions, source and `use` line |
| `vyrn add <name>`, `vyrn add <name>@v2` | fetches and locks it |
| `vyrn fetch` | downloads everything in `vyrn.lock`, to work offline |

## Publishing a package

1. Fill in the registry fields of `vyrn.toml`:

   ```toml
   [package]
   name = "greeter"
   edition = "2026"
   main = "main.vyrn"
   version = "1.0.0"
   description = "Friendly greetings"
   repository = "github.com/you/greeter"
   keywords = "greeting, example"
   license = "MIT"
   ```

2. Commit, tag the version, and push both:

   ```bash
   git tag v1.0.0
   ```

   ```bash
   git push origin main v1.0.0
   ```

3. Fork Vyrn's repository (`github.com/Dmccottrell/Vyrn`), whose
   `registry` folder is the registry, clone your fork next to your
   package, and from the package's folder:

   ```bash
   vyrn publish --to ../Vyrn/registry
   ```

   It runs `vyrn check` and your tests, makes sure the tag exists, and adds
   the entry to `registry/index.json`. Commit that and open a pull
   request. Without `--to`, it writes `registry-entry.json` for you to
   paste in.

## How the registry works

The registry is one file, `registry/index.json` in Vyrn's repository,
published by the Learn Vyrn website and listed on its Packages page. It
maps names to repositories and lists their versions; no code is stored
there, and no server runs. CI checks every change with
`registry/check.vyrn` (names, URLs and version tags).
`tools/registry-template/` is the starting point for a registry of your
own (a company's, say).

`VYRN_REGISTRY` points `vyrn` at another index, a URL or a file, for a
private or company registry. Without a network, `vyrn search` uses the copy
it downloaded last.

title: Debugging
blurb: Finding bugs: the debugger and VS Code.
text:
# Debugging

A debugger stops your program while it runs, so you can look inside it:
which line it is on, what every variable holds, and which function called
which. Use it when a program does something you didn't expect. Instead of
adding `print` everywhere, stop it and look.

## In VS Code

1. Open a `.vyrn` file.
2. Click in the margin left of a line number to set a **breakpoint**. A red
   dot appears there, and the program stops when it gets to that line.
3. Press **F5**, or run **Vyrn: Debug File** from the command palette.

When the program stops, the line is highlighted and the side bar shows:

- **Variables**: everything in scope, under *Locals*, and the program's
  top-level values, under *Globals*. Click the arrow beside a list, map
  or object to open it.
- **Call stack**: the function you are in, and the calls that led there.
  Click a line to see that function's variables.
- **Watch**: type a name such as `player.pos.x` or `scores[0]` to keep
  an eye on it.

Hovering over a variable in the editor shows its value. The buttons at the
top control what happens next:

| Button | Key | Does |
|---|---|---|
| Continue | F5 | run to the next breakpoint |
| Step Over | F10 | run this line, then stop at the next (a function it calls runs without stopping) |
| Step Into | F11 | go into the function this line calls |
| Step Out | Shift+F11 | finish this function, and stop in the one that called it |
| Stop | Shift+F5 | end the program |

What `print` shows appears in the **Debug Console**.

To pass arguments, or to stop at the first line every time, add a
`.vscode/launch.json`:

```json
{
  "version": "0.2.0",
  "configurations": [
    {
      "type": "vyrn",
      "request": "launch",
      "name": "Debug the game",
      "program": "${workspaceFolder}/main.vyrn",
      "args": ["--level", "2"],
      "stopOnEntry": true
    }
  ]
}
```

## In the terminal

```bash
vyrn debug score.vyrn
```

The program stops at its first line and waits for a command:

```
Debugging. Type `help` for the commands.
-> score.vyrn:12 in main
   12 |     var players = [Player("Ann", 3), Player("Bo", 5)]
(vyrn) break 7
breakpoint at score.vyrn:7
(vyrn) continue
-> breakpoint, score.vyrn:7 in bonus
   7 |     let doubled = points * 2
(vyrn) print points
points = 3
(vyrn) where
-> bonus at score.vyrn:7
   main at score.vyrn:15
```

| Command | Short | Does |
|---|---|---|
| `next` | `n` | run to the next line, stepping over calls |
| `step` | `s` | run to the next line, going into calls |
| `out` | `o` | run until this function returns |
| `continue` | `c` | run to the next breakpoint |
| `break 12`, `break other.vyrn:12` | `b` | stop at that line |
| `delete 12` | | remove that breakpoint |
| `print x`, `print player.pos.x`, `print items[0]` | `p` | show a value; lists, maps and objects show their parts |
| `vars` | `v` | every variable here |
| `where` | `w` | the calls that led here |
| `list` | `l` | the code around this line |
| `quit` | `q` | stop the program |
| Enter | | repeat the last command |

## How it works

`vyrn debug` runs the program on the interpreter. Before each instruction
it checks whether it has reached a new line, and if so whether it should
stop there: a breakpoint, the end of a step, or a pause. Functions that
normally run as machine code run on the interpreter while debugging, so
every line can be stopped at. Programs therefore run slower in the
debugger than under `vyrn run`.

`vyrn debug --dap` speaks the
[Debug Adapter Protocol](https://microsoft.github.io/debug-adapter-protocol/)
on standard input and output. That is how the VS Code extension uses it,
and any editor with a DAP client (Neovim, Emacs, Zed and others) can use it
the same way.

title: Tensors and the GPU
text:
# `vyrn.nn` Kernels: Vyrn Code on the GPU

Status: element-wise kernels **run today** on the CPU and, with
`--features gpu`, as generated WGSL compute shaders (`src/vm/kernel.rs`,
`src/vm/gpu.rs`). Tile kernels (section 4), which a custom attention
mechanism needs, are design. Each section says which applies.

## 1. The model a developer learns

A `kernel` function is written on numbers. Called with numbers, it is an ordinary
function. Called with tensors, it runs once per element, on whichever
device the tensors live on. That is all there is to learn (rule 2, the
five-minute test):

```vyrn
const BETA = 1.5

## Swish with a sharpness: x * sigmoid(beta * x).
kernel create swish(x: f32, beta: f32) -> f32:
    let gate = 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-beta * x))
    return x * gate
end

kernel create mix(a: f32, b: f32, t: f32) -> f32:
    return a + (b - a) * t
end

main:
    print(swish(1.0, BETA))                     # a number: 0.8175744761936437

    on gpu[0]:
        let h = rand(4096, 4096) * 8.0 - 4.0
        let y = swish(h, BETA)                  # one compute shader, 16.7M threads
        let z = mix(h, y, 0.25)                 # a second one
        print(z.shape)
    end
end
```

Arguments may mix tensors (all of one shape, on one device) and numbers
(the same for every element). The checker knows the rule: an `f32`
parameter accepts a tensor, and the call's result is then a tensor.

A kernel body is `let` bindings followed by one `return`, using
`+ - * / **`, unary `-`, comparisons, `a if c else b`, numeric constants,
and `exp`, `tanh`, `sqrt`, `abs`, `relu`, `gelu`, `min`, `max`. A body that
does more still works on numbers, and calling it on a tensor says exactly
why it cannot run there:

```text
error: kernel `noisy` works on numbers, but cannot run on tensors because
       its body is not `let` bindings followed by one `return`
```

## 2. How a kernel becomes WGSL

```text
kernel create swish(...)      syntax tree (FnDecl, `kernel` modifier)
        │  src/vm/kernel.rs: lower()
        ▼
Kernel IR                     params, let-bound locals, one result expression
  l0 = 1 / (1 + exp(-p1 * p0))
  result = p0 * l0
        │                        │
        │ wgsl(arg pattern)      │ run_cpu()
        ▼                        ▼
WGSL compute shader           direct evaluation over the elements
        │  src/vm/gpu.rs: compiled once per (kernel, tensor/number pattern), cached
        ▼
dispatch: one invocation per element, 64 per workgroup
```

1. **Lowering.** At compile time, every `kernel` function body is lowered to a
   small expression IR: parameters, `let` locals in order, one result.
   Names resolve to parameters, earlier locals, or numeric constants, which
   are folded in. The IR is stored with the function (`Proto::kernel`), or
   the reason it could not be lowered.
2. **Dispatch.** A call with any tensor argument takes the VM's rarely-used
   call path, shared with `async` function, so ordinary calls pay nothing for it.
   It checks shapes and devices and asks the tensors' backend to run the
   kernel. The reference backend declines, and the IR is evaluated on the
   CPU.
3. **WGSL generation.** The GPU backend generates a shader for the pattern
   of arguments (which are tensors, which are numbers). Tensors become
   read-only storage buffers, numbers one `scalars` buffer, and each IR
   node one WGSL expression. `vyrn bytecode` prints it; this is `swish`:

   ```wgsl
   @group(0) @binding(0) var<storage, read_write> out: array<f32>;
   @group(0) @binding(1) var<storage, read> scalars: array<f32>;
   @group(0) @binding(2) var<uniform> sizes: Sizes;
   @group(0) @binding(3) var<storage, read> input0: array<f32>;
   @compute @workgroup_size(64)
   fn main(@builtin(global_invocation_id) gid: vec3<u32>, @builtin(num_workgroups) groups: vec3<u32>) {
       let i = gid.x + gid.y * groups.x * 64u;
       if (i >= sizes.len) { return; }
       let p0 = input0[i];
       let p1 = scalars[0u];
       let l0 = (f32(1.0) / (f32(1.0) + exp(((-p1) * p0))));
       out[i] = (p0 * l0);
   }
   ```

4. **Compilation and caching.** The shader is compiled once per source text
   and cached, so a kernel in a training or decode loop is compiled on its
   first call only. Work under 4,096 elements stays on the CPU, where it is
   cheaper than a dispatch.

**Same results everywhere.** Both paths compute in `f32` from the same IR.
`tanh` is clamped to ±15 (where it is already ±1 in `f32`) because some
drivers return NaN past that, and `gelu` uses the same tanh approximation
on both. `tests/gpu.rs` runs a kernel using every construct on the GPU and
the CPU and requires agreement to 1e-4 relative.

## 3. Memory layout and cache locality

What the GPU sees is decided by how tensors are stored, and Vyrn keeps that
simple enough to guarantee:

1. **Every tensor is dense and row-major.** There are no strided views:
   slicing, transposing (`.T`) and placement produce new contiguous tensors.
   Element `[i, j]` of an `[m, n]` tensor is at `i * n + j`, always. A
   kernel thread `i` therefore reads element `i` of each input, and the 64
   threads of a workgroup read 64 consecutive values: one coalesced memory
   transaction per input.
2. **Python memory must be contiguous too.** `x.to_tensor()` refuses a
   non-contiguous NumPy view with a fix (`np.ascontiguousarray(x)`) rather
   than taking strides that would break rule 1 (`docs/ffi.md`).
3. **Quantized weights are blocks along rows.** `q8` and `q4` (llama.cpp's
   Q8_0 and Q4_0) store 32 consecutive values per block, with one `f16`
   scale per block. A block never crosses a row when the row length is a
   multiple of 32, which holds for every transformer dimension (4096, 5120,
   13824, ...). `q4` packs two values per byte, low nibble first, so the 8
   values a 32-bit word holds are consecutive in a row.
4. **Weights go to the GPU packed, and stay.** A `q4` matrix is uploaded as
   its packed bytes plus a separate scales buffer, and decoded in the
   shader. 4-bit weights take 4-bit memory in VRAM and on the bus. Matrices
   of 256 KB or more stay resident until the tensor is dropped.
5. **Reads are coalesced in the matrix product.** For `x @ w` with `w` of
   shape `[k, n]`, thread `j` computes output column `j` and reads `w[p, j]`
   for each `p`. Neighbouring threads read neighbouring values, which for
   `q4` are neighbouring nibbles of the same 32-bit word, under one shared
   block scale. During decoding (`m = 1`, the case that dominates LLM
   inference), each weight byte is read from memory once per token.
6. **Buffers are 4-byte aligned and padded**, as WGSL storage arrays
   require. Odd-length `q4` data is padded with zero nibbles that no
   thread reads.

## 4. Design: tile kernels for attention

Element-wise kernels cover activations, gates, residual mixing, scaling and
masks. A custom attention mechanism also needs reductions and index
arithmetic. The design extends `kernel` function rather than adding a second
mechanism (rule 1):

```vyrn
## Scores for grouped-query attention: q is [T, D], k is [S, D].
kernel create scores(q: tensor[f16; T, D], k: tensor[q8; S, D], scale: f32) -> tensor[f32; T, S]:
    each t, s in grid(T, S):              # one GPU invocation per output element
        var acc = 0.0
        each d in 0 until D:              # a loop inside the invocation
            acc += q[t, d] * k[s, d]
        end
        out[t, s] = acc * scale if s <= t else -1e30   # causal mask, fused
    end
end

main:
    on gpu[0]:
        let p = softmax(scores(q, k, 0.088), axis = -1) @ v
    end
end
```

How it lowers:

| Vyrn | WGSL |
|---|---|
| `each t, s in grid(T, S)` (outermost, once) | the dispatch grid: `global_invocation_id.xy`, with a bounds check |
| `each d in 0 until D` | a WGSL `for` loop |
| `q[t, d]` on `f16` / `f32` | `q[t * D + d]` (row-major, section 3), widened to `f32` |
| `k[s, d]` on `q8` / `q4` | the block decoder the matrix product shader already uses: `load_b(s * D + d)` |
| `out[t, s] = ...` | the single write of the invocation |
| dimension names `T, S, D` | uniforms filled from the argument shapes, checked against each other before dispatch |

Then three optimizations, each invisible in the source:

1. **Tiling.** When the inner loop reads one input along the reduction
   axis (here `d`), the compiler stages 16 × 16 tiles of both inputs in
   workgroup shared memory, the standard matmul tiling.
2. **Epilogue fusion.** An element-wise `kernel` function applied to a tile
   kernel's result (`swish(x @ w)`) is inlined into that kernel's final
   write, so the intermediate tensor never reaches memory.
3. **Static checks.** The `kernel` modifier already implies `strict`: the
   checker requires typed parameters, so an index out of a declared shape,
   or a `T` used for two sizes, is an error before anything runs.

The order of work: `grid` and inner loops on the CPU evaluator (so every
kernel has an exact reference), then WGSL generation, then tiling, then
fusion.

## 5. What `vyrn.nn` builds on this

The layers in `docs/stdlib.md` (`nn.Linear`, `nn.RMSNorm`, `nn.Attention`,
`nn.MLP`) become ordinary Vyrn code: structs holding weight tensors, and
`forward` methods built from `@` and `kernel` functions. Developers read and copy
them like any other code, and a custom layer is the same kind of code as a
built-in one.

title: C and Python
text:
# Foreign Code and Decentralized Modules

Vyrn reaches three kinds of code outside itself:

| Component | Vyrn syntax | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Embedded CPython | `use python.datasets` | runs (`--features python`) | `src/vm/python.rs`, `src/vm/python_tensor.rs` |
| Zero-copy tensors from Python | `array.to_tensor()` | runs | `src/vm/dtype.rs` (`External`), `src/vm/python_tensor.rs` |
| C and C++ libraries | `@link("m")` + `extern "c":` | runs (`--features ffi`) | `src/vm/ffi.rs`, `src/check.rs` |
| Modules from any git host | `use "github.com/ann/neural@v1"` | runs (default) | `src/project/` |

The two bridges plug into the VM through one trait, `Foreign`
(`src/vm/foreign.rs`): attribute access, calls, indexing, `len`, iteration
and operators. A build without a bridge has the same VM, and a program that
uses one gets an error saying which feature to build with.

Every snippet below is taken, shortened, from the code; the tests that
exercise it are `tests/bridges.rs` and `tests/project.rs`.

---

## 1. The CPython embed

### 1.1 Shape

CPython runs inside the `vyrn` process (through PyO3, linked against the
system's `libpython`), started on the first `use python.*`. A call into
Python is a function call, not a message to another process. Vyrn is
single-threaded, so each call attaches to the interpreter for its duration
(`Python::attach`), and nothing else holds the GIL.

Rule 1 applies: module paths use dots everywhere, so it is
`use python.datasets`, never `use python::datasets`.

### 1.2 From `use` to the C API

```vyrn
use python.datasets

main:
    let ds = datasets.load_dataset("imdb", split = "train")
    print(len(ds))
end
```

**Parse.** `use python.datasets` is an ordinary `UseDecl` with path
`[python, datasets]`.

**Compile.** The compiler turns a Python import into a global that is
filled before anything else runs (`src/vm/compiler.rs`):

```rust
/// `use python.numpy as np`, `use python.os.path (join)`.
fn python_use(&mut self, decl: &UseDecl, path: &[&str]) {
    let module = Value::str(path.join("."));
    match &decl.kind {
        UseKind::Module { alias } => {
            let local = alias.as_ref().map_or(path[path.len() - 1], |a| a.name.as_str());
            self.foreign_global(local, decl.path.span, "python.import", vec![module]);
        }
        UseKind::Names(names) => {
            for n in names {
                let local = n.alias.as_ref().unwrap_or(&n.name).name.clone();
                self.foreign_global(&local, n.name.span, "python.import",
                    vec![module.clone(), Value::str(n.name.name.clone())]);
            }
        }
    }
}
```

**Bytecode.** `vyrn bytecode` shows the result. The module initializer
calls the `python.import` builtin and stores the module in a global; `main`
calls a method on it with a keyword argument:

```text
fn #1 <module>() registers=2
    k0 = Native(47)              ; python.import
    k1 = Str("datasets")
     0  LoadConst { dst: 0, k: 0 }
     1  LoadConst { dst: 1, k: 1 }
     2  Call { func: 0, argc: 1 }
     3  SetGlobal { src: 0, idx: 0 }

fn #0 main() registers=6
     0  GetGlobal { dst: 2, idx: 0 }                    ; datasets
     1  LoadConst { dst: 3, k: 0 }                      ; "imdb"
     2  LoadConst { dst: 4, k: 1 }                      ; "train"
     3  LoadConst { dst: 5, k: 2 }                      ; ("split",)
     4  CallMethodKw { base: 1, argc: 2, name: 0 }      ; .load_dataset
```

**Run.** `python.import` is `PyImport_ImportModule`; `CallMethodKw` on a
foreign receiver becomes `PyObject_Call` on the attribute, with a tuple of
positional arguments and a dict of keyword arguments:

```rust
pub fn import(module: &str, name: Option<&str>) -> VmResult<Value> {
    Python::attach(|py| {
        let m = py.import(module).map_err(|e| python_error(py, e))?;   // PyImport_ImportModule
        let object = match name {
            Some(n) => m.getattr(n).map_err(|e| python_error(py, e))?, // PyObject_GetAttr
            None => m.into_any(),
        };
        Ok(from_python(&object))
    })
}

impl Foreign for PyValue {
    fn call_method(&self, _: &mut Ctx, name: &str, args: &[Value], kwargs: &[(String, Value)]) -> VmResult<Value> {
        Python::attach(|py| {
            let (args, kwargs) = args_kwargs(py, args, kwargs)?;        // PyTuple + PyDict
            self.object.bind(py)
                .call_method(name, args, kwargs.as_ref())                // PyObject_Call
                .map(|v| from_python(&v))
                .map_err(|e| python_error(py, e))
        })
    }
    // get_attr, call, index, len, items, binary (+ - * / // % **), equals, truthy
}
```

### 1.3 The type boundary

| Vyrn | Python | Back to Vyrn |
|---|---|---|
| `none`, `bool`, `int`, `float`, `str` | same | converted |
| `[T]`, `(A, B)`, `{K: V}` | `list`, `tuple`, `dict` | stay Python objects |
| `tensor` | `memoryview` of float32, accepted by NumPy and PyTorch | see section 2 |
| Python object | the object itself | a Python object |

Python containers stay Python objects on the way back: `len`, `x[i]`,
`each`, attributes and operators work on them directly, and nothing is
converted until the program asks (rule 4). A Python exception becomes a
Vyrn failure of kind `PythonError` whose message starts with the Python
class: `catch PythonError as e`. A missing module says how to install it:

```text
error: Python has no module `datasets`; install it with `python3 -m pip install datasets`
```

Packages come from the Python that `vyrn` was linked against. A project-local
environment (`[python] venv = ".venv"` in `vyrn.toml`, put on `sys.path`
at start-up) is the next step.

---

## 2. The zero-copy tensor bridge

### 2.1 Requirement

A tensor that came from Python must be usable in Vyrn's native matrix code
without copying its data, while keeping Vyrn's guarantees: memory is never
freed underneath a tensor, and changing a tensor never changes someone
else's.

### 2.2 Borrowed storage

A tensor's storage can be memory owned by someone else
(`src/vm/dtype.rs`):

```rust
/// Memory that belongs to someone else, such as a NumPy array or a
/// memory-mapped file, read in place.
pub struct External {
    ptr: *const u8,
    bytes: usize,
    dtype: DType,                              // f32, f16 or bf16
    _owner: Rc<dyn Any>,                       // keeps the memory alive
}

impl External {
    /// # Safety
    /// The memory must stay valid, and must not be freed or resized, for as
    /// long as `owner` is alive.
    pub unsafe fn new(ptr: *const u8, bytes: usize, dtype: DType,
                      owner: Rc<dyn Any>) -> Option<External> { /* checks alignment and length */ }

    pub fn f32s(&self) -> &[f32] {
        // SAFETY: `new`'s contract keeps the memory valid while `_owner` lives.
        unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts(self.ptr as *const f32, self.bytes / 4) }
    }
}

pub enum Storage {
    F32(Vec<f32>), F16(Vec<u16>), BF16(Vec<u16>), Quantized(Quantized),
    External(Rc<External>),
}
```

Every reader (matrix products, element-wise math, the GPU upload, the
weights writer) reads `External` memory directly; `values()` returns it as a
borrowed slice. Writing is copy on write:

```rust
pub fn data_mut(&mut self) -> Result<&mut Vec<f32>, TensorError> {
    // Borrowed memory is copied into Vyrn's own on the first change.
    if let Storage::External(e) = &self.storage {
        if e.dtype() == DType::F32 {
            self.storage = Storage::F32(e.f32s().to_vec());
        }
    }
    ...
}
```

### 2.3 Taking a Python buffer

Python's buffer protocol is the common ground: NumPy arrays, `memoryview`,
`array.array` and PyTorch CPU tensors (through `.numpy()`) all describe
their memory with a pointer, a shape and an element format. Vyrn holds the
buffer, which pins the exporter's memory, and stores it as the owner
(`src/vm/python_tensor.rs`):

```rust
pub fn tensor_from_python(py: Python<'_>, object: &Bound<'_, PyAny>) -> VmResult<Value> {
    let buffer = PyUntypedBuffer::get(&object)?;                  // PyObject_GetBuffer
    let dtype = match buffer.format() { "f" => DType::F32, "e" => DType::F16, other => refuse(other)? };
    if !buffer.is_c_contiguous() { refuse_noncontiguous()? }
    let shape = buffer.shape().to_vec();
    let (ptr, bytes) = (buffer.buf_ptr() as *const u8, buffer.len_bytes());
    let owner: Rc<dyn Any> = Rc::new(buffer);                    // PyBuffer_Release on drop
    // SAFETY: a held Python buffer keeps the exporter's memory valid and its
    // size fixed until it is released, which happens when `owner` is dropped.
    let storage = Storage::External(Rc::new(unsafe { External::new(ptr, bytes, dtype, owner) }?));
    Ok(Value::Tensor(Rc::new(DeviceTensor::new(Tensor { shape, storage, device: Device::Cpu }))))
}
```

What the tests check: a change NumPy makes in place is visible through the
tensor; a write through Vyrn copies first and leaves NumPy's array alone; a
tensor outlives the NumPy array it came from; a 1000 × 1000 array goes
straight into `@`.

### 2.4 Python types to Vyrn tensors

| Python | Vyrn | Copy? |
|---|---|---|
| contiguous `float32` array | `tensor[f32]` | none |
| contiguous `float16` array | `tensor[f16]` | none |
| PyTorch CPU tensor | through `.numpy()`, as above | none |
| `float64`, integer arrays | refused: "convert it with `.astype("float32")`" | the program decides |
| non-contiguous view | refused: "pass `np.ascontiguousarray(x)`" | the program decides |
| big-endian array | refused | the program decides |
| `bfloat16` (PyTorch) | planned: `.view(torch.int16)` exported as raw `bf16` | none |

Refusing, rather than silently converting, is rule 4: a copy of a large
array is a cost the program should see.

### 2.5 Hugging Face to native matrix code

```vyrn
use python.datasets
use python.numpy as np

main:
    # Hugging Face downloads and caches the dataset; any dataset with an
    # `embedding` column of float32 vectors works the same way.
    let ds = datasets.load_dataset("your-org/imdb-embeddings", split = "train")
    let rows = ds.with_format("numpy")["embedding"]          # (n, 768) float32
    let x = np.ascontiguousarray(rows, dtype = "float32").to_tensor()

    # From here on everything is native Vyrn, on the GPU if there is one.
    on gpu[0]:
        let w1 = rand(768, 256) * 0.02
        let w2 = rand(256, 2) * 0.02
        let logits = gelu((x on gpu[0]) @ w1) @ w2
        print(logits.shape, softmax(logits, axis = -1)[0])
    end
end
```

`x` shares the dataset's memory: no byte is copied between Python and the
matrix product. Moving it with `on gpu[0]` is the one copy, and it is
written in the source.

**Safetensors files** take the same path through Python
(`safetensors.numpy.load_file(path)` gives NumPy arrays), and Vyrn's own
`load_weights` reads them natively. The next step is for `load_weights` to
memory-map the file and hand out `External` tensors over the mapping, which
reaches the same zero-copy result without Python (the `vyrn.fs.map` design
in `docs/stdlib.md`).

---

## 3. The C and C++ bridge

### 3.1 Declaring C functions

```vyrn
@link("accel")                       # libaccel.so / accel.dll; omit for libc
extern "c":
    create accel_sum(x: tensor[f32], n: i32) -> f32
    create accel_new() -> ptr u8
    create accel_add(h: ptr u8, x: tensor[f32], n: i32)
    create accel_free(h: ptr u8)
end

main:
    let x = arange(1024)
    unsafe:
        print(accel_sum(x, 1024))
        let h = accel_new()
        accel_add(h, x, 1024)
        accel_free(h)
    end
end
```

**Compile.** Each declaration becomes a signature string checked at compile
time. A type that cannot cross is an error with a fix, not a crash:

```rust
/// A C function's signature in the form the FFI builtin reads: `f64(f64,ptr)`.
fn c_signature(f: &FnDecl) -> Result<String, (String, Span)> { ... }
// accel_add  ->  "void(ptr,ptr,i32)"
```

**Run.** At start-up the library is opened (`libloading`), the symbol found,
and a libffi call description (`Cif`) prepared. A call converts each
argument to its C type, range-checking integers, and calls through libffi
(`src/vm/ffi.rs`):

```rust
let slots: Vec<Slot> = self.params.iter().zip(args).enumerate()
    .map(|(i, (&ty, v))| self.convert(i, ty, v, &mut strings))   // i32 range checks, CString, tensor pointer
    .collect::<VmResult<_>>()?;
let ffi_args: Vec<Arg> = slots.iter().map(Slot::arg).collect();
// SAFETY: `cif` describes the declared signature, every argument was
// converted to exactly that C type, and the pointers in `slots` (strings,
// tensor data) stay alive until the call returns.
unsafe { self.cif.call::<f32>(self.code, &ffi_args) }
```

| Vyrn | C |
|---|---|
| `int` | `i8` ... `u64` (out-of-range values are an `OverflowError`) |
| `float` | `f32`, `f64` |
| `bool` | `_Bool` |
| `str` | `const char*`, NUL-terminated, valid for the call |
| `tensor[f32]` | `float*` to its data, valid for the call |
| C pointer, `none` | `void*`, `NULL` |

### 3.2 The borrow checker and raw pointers

Vyrn's borrow checking is function-local and has no lifetime annotations
(`docs/architecture.md`), so raw pointers are kept out of the safe language
instead of being tracked through it:

1. **Pointers into Vyrn memory never become values.** A tensor or string
   passed to C is converted to a pointer inside the call and the pointer is
   gone when the call returns. Nothing in Vyrn can hold it, store it or
   return it, so there is nothing to track.
2. **Pointers from C are opaque handles** (`ptr u8`). Vyrn can compare them,
   pass them back to C and check them against `none`, but cannot read
   through them. The memory belongs to the C library, which also frees it.
3. **Calls that pass or return pointers go in `unsafe:`.** The checker
   enforces it (`src/check.rs`):

   ```text
   error: `accel_add` passes raw pointers to C, so it can only be called in an `unsafe:` block
     = help: put the call in `unsafe:` ... `end`: you promise the C code reads and
             writes only what it was given, and keeps no pointer to Vyrn memory after it returns
   ```

   Functions that take and return only numbers, such as `cos`, are safe to
   call anywhere: no memory crosses.
4. **`mut` marks writes.** A C parameter declared `mut x: tensor[f32]` needs
   `mut x` at the call, so the existing rules apply: the argument must be a
   `var`, and it cannot also appear elsewhere in the same call.

One gap remains: C writing through a tensor pointer is visible to every
variable sharing that tensor, because the bridge does not yet give a `mut`
tensor argument its own copy before the call. Until it does, pass `mut`
tensors that are not shared.

### 3.3 Headers and C++

Hand-written `extern` blocks are the one mechanism (rule 1). Header import
is a tool that writes them: `vyrn bind accel.h > accel.vyrn` (design) parses
the header with libclang and emits one `extern "c":` block, mapping
`float*` to `tensor[f32]` or `ptr f32` by an annotation table. C++ is
reached through its C ABI: an `extern "C"` header of free functions over
opaque handles, the same pattern CUDA, cuBLAS and most accelerator SDKs
already ship. Calling C++ classes directly is not planned.

---

## 4. The decentralized module resolver

### 4.1 Syntax and versions

```vyrn
use "github.com/Dmccottrell/A.I-SML@v3" as yuvra
use "codeberg.org/ann/models/llama@v2.1"          # a directory inside a repository
use "gitlab.com/lab/tokenizers@main"              # a branch
```

| Version | Means |
|---|---|
| `@v3` | the newest tag `v3.x.y` |
| `@v3.1` | the newest tag `v3.1.y` |
| `@v3.1.2` | exactly that tag |
| `@main` | the newest commit on branch `main` |
| `@3f9c2e1...` (40 hex digits) | exactly that commit |

Without `as`, a module is bound to its last path segment, made into an
identifier (`A.I-SML` becomes `A_I_SML`). A module's entry point is
`lib.vyrn`; its own `use a.b` lines are relative to its directory.

There is no registry: the `use` line is the dependency (one place to write
it), and `vyrn.lock` records exactly what it resolved to (one place that
records it). `vyrn add <url>` resolves ahead of time and `vyrn fetch` fills
the cache for offline work.

### 4.2 The fetch and cache loop

Tags and branches are listed with git's own HTTPS protocol (the "smart
HTTP" ref advertisement), which every git host speaks, so any host works
without a special API. An archive of the chosen commit is downloaded,
unpacked in memory, hashed by content, and stored in a content-addressed
cache (`src/project/resolve.rs`):

```rust
pub fn resolve(&mut self, text: &str) -> Result<PathBuf, String> {
    let url = ModuleUrl::parse(text).map_err(|e| e.0)?;            // host, repo, subdir, version
    let root = match self.lock.modules.get(text).cloned() {
        Some(locked) => {
            let dir = self.cache.join(&locked.hash);                // ~/.vyrn/modules/sha256-…
            if !dir.is_dir() {
                if self.offline { return Err(not_cached(text)); }
                let tree = self.download(&url, &locked.commit)?;
                let hash = tree_hash(&tree);
                if hash != locked.hash {
                    return Err(format!("`{text}` changed since it was locked: commit {} now hashes \
                        to {hash}, but vyrn.lock says {}", locked.commit, locked.hash));
                }
                self.store(&tree, &hash)?;
            }
            dir
        }
        None => {
            if self.offline { return Err(not_locked(text)); }
            let refs = self.fetcher.list_refs(&url)?;               // GET /info/refs?service=git-upload-pack
            let (version, commit) = select(&url.version, &refs)     // newest matching tag
                .ok_or_else(|| no_match(&url, &refs))?;
            let tree = self.download(&url, &commit)?;               // archive of that commit, unpacked
            let hash = tree_hash(&tree);
            let dir = self.store(&tree, &hash)?;                    // unpack beside, then rename
            self.lock.modules.insert(text.to_string(), Locked { version, commit, hash });
            self.lock_changed = true;
            dir
        }
    };
    Ok(match &url.subdir { Some(sub) => root.join(sub), None => root })
}
```

The hash covers the files, not the archive, so it is the same from any
mirror and does not depend on how the host compresses archives:

```rust
pub fn tree_hash(tree: &Tree) -> String {
    let mut h = Sha256::new();
    for (path, data) in tree {                                     // sorted by path
        h.update((path.len() as u64).to_le_bytes()); h.update(path.as_bytes());
        h.update((data.len() as u64).to_le_bytes()); h.update(data);
    }
    format!("sha256-{}", hex(h.finalize()))
}
```

```text
# vyrn.lock: written by vyrn. Commit it; do not edit it.

[[module]]
url = "github.com/Dmccottrell/A.I-SML@v3"
version = "v3.1.0"
commit = "dddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddd"
hash = "sha256-…"
```

**Security properties.**
