- HTTPS only; `HTTPS_PROXY` and `SSL_CERT_FILE` are honoured, for corporate
  networks.
- Nothing runs on install: a module is source code, never a build or
  install script.
- Archives are unpacked in memory. Links and devices are skipped, and any
  path that would land outside the module (`..`, absolute paths) aborts the
  whole module.
- A locked module whose bytes change is refused, even under the same commit
  and even from the original host. Accepting new code takes an explicit
  `vyrn add`.
- The cache is written beside its final place and renamed, so a crash never
  leaves half a module.

### 4.3 Linking at compile time

Fetched modules join the program at the syntax-tree level, before checking
and bytecode generation (`src/project/loader.rs`):

1. **Load.** Starting from the main file, each `use` is located: the
   standard library and `python.*` are left to the compiler; local
   `use a.b` is `a/b.vyrn` under the project; a URL is resolved as above and
   its `lib.vyrn` loaded. Each file is parsed at its own base offset
   (`file index << 24`), so every span records which file it came from and
   errors name the right file.
2. **Namespace.** Each file gets a prefix (`yuvra`, `geo.shapes`). Its
   top-level declarations are renamed into it, so two modules can both
   declare `load`.
3. **Rewrite references.** A scope-aware pass rewrites each name to the
   declaration it means: the file's own names, names imported with
   `use m (a, b as c)`, and `module.member` collapsed to one name (in
   expressions, types, patterns and decorators). Local variables are
   tracked, so a variable is never mistaken for an import of the same name.
   A missing member is an error at this point: `module `yuvra` has no
   `train``.
4. **Merge.** The files' items become one module, dependencies first, and
   go through the checker and compiler as if they were one file.

### 4.4 Offline mode

After the first fetch, a project builds with no network:

| State | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Locked and cached | No network access at all; the cache answers. |
| Locked, not cached (new machine) | Downloads that exact commit and verifies the hash. With `VYRN_OFFLINE=1`: "run `vyrn fetch` while online". |
| Not locked | Resolves and locks. With `VYRN_OFFLINE=1`: "run `vyrn add <url>` while online". |

`vyrn fetch` downloads every locked module, for machines that will be
offline later, and `vyrn build` bundles every fetched module into the
executable, so a built program needs neither the network nor the cache.

### 4.5 Tested

`tests/project.rs` runs the resolver against an in-memory git host:
resolving `@v1` to the newest `v1.x.y`, writing `vyrn.lock`, answering from
the cache offline after a newer version is published, refusing a rewritten
commit, listing the existing tags when none match, `as yuvra` with
`A.I-SML@v3`, namespaces, and errors that name their file.
`tests/net.rs` (`cargo test --test net -- --ignored`) runs the HTTPS fetcher
against a real public repository. In the sandbox this was developed in, the
ref listing from github.com worked and the archive host
(`codeload.github.com`) was blocked by the sandbox's network policy (`curl`
gets the same 403), so the archive download has been verified only through
the in-memory host.

title: Deploying
text:
# Deploying Vyrn: Cloud Binaries and Edge WebAssembly

One program, two kinds of place to run it:

| | Cloud (servers, GPU instances) | Edge (Vercel, Cloudflare, Deno, browsers) |
|---|---|---|
| Command | `vyrn build --target=linux-musl` | `vyrn build --target=wasm32-edge` |
| Output | one static Linux executable | a directory: `vyrn.wasm`, the program, a few lines of JavaScript |
| Runs today | the bytecode VM with the program bundled; typed functions as machine code (section 3) | the bytecode VM compiled to WebAssembly |
| Next | lists, structs and strings in native code; an LLVM release tier (section 4) | the same, through the WebAssembly backend |

Both builds run the same source. `examples/api.vyrn` serves the same
responses from `vyrn run`, from a static Linux binary, and from the edge
build driven with web `Request` objects.

## 1. Compiler flags

```text
vyrn build [file] [-o out] [--target=T]
```

| `--target` | Builds | Uses |
|---|---|---|
| `native` (default) | an executable for this machine | the running `vyrn` |
| `linux-gnu` | x86-64 Linux, glibc | runtime for `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` |
| `linux-musl` | x86-64 Linux, fully static: runs on any distribution, in `FROM scratch` containers | `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` |
| `linux-arm64` | ARM64 Linux (Graviton, Ampere, Jetson) | `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` |
| `macos`, `macos-intel`, `windows` | desktop systems | `aarch64-apple-darwin`, `x86_64-apple-darwin`, `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` |
| any Rust target triple | that system | the runtime built for it |
| `wasm32-edge` | an edge deployment directory | `vyrn.wasm` |

Runtimes for other targets are looked up in `$VYRN_RUNTIMES` (default
`~/.vyrn/runtimes/<triple>/vyrn`, and `runtimes/wasm32/vyrn.wasm`). A
missing one is an error that gives the command to build it:

```bash
cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl --no-default-features
```

```bash
cargo build --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --manifest-path runtime/wasm/Cargo.toml
```

Runtimes leave out the module fetcher (`--no-default-features`): a built
program carries all its modules, so it never fetches anything. This also
keeps the musl build free of C code (the TLS library is the only C in the
default build).

## 2. What exists today

### 2.1 Cloud: static executables

`vyrn build` appends the program (every source file it loads, URL modules
included) to a copy of the `vyrn` runtime for the target, followed by the
bundle's length and a marker (`src/project/bundle.rs`). At start-up the
runtime finds the marker at the end of its own file and runs the program.
The musl runtime is a 3.2 MB `static-pie` executable with no dynamic
dependencies at all.

What this gives cloud GPU instances today: the tensor work (`@`, kernels,
`on gpu[0]`) runs in the GPU backend (`--features gpu`) and in native Rust,
so a large model's inference loop spends its time in native code. Only the
glue between tensor operations is interpreted. Section 3 removes that last
layer.

### 2.2 Edge: WebAssembly

`runtime/wasm` compiles the whole toolchain (parser, checker, compiler,
VM, with SQLite and HTML parsing) to `wasm32-unknown-unknown`: a 3.8 MB
module (about 1.4 MB compressed) with **no imports**, so
any WebAssembly host can load it. Its interface is plain memory and
integers (`vyrn_run`, `vyrn_load`, `vyrn_handle`, `vyrn_set_time`,
`vyrn_seed`), and
`runtime/wasm/vyrn-edge.mjs` wraps it in the web platform's own types:

```js
const vyrn = await loadVyrn(wasmModule);
const handle = vyrn.serve(programBytes);   // (Request) => Promise<Response>
```

`vyrn build --target=wasm32-edge` writes:

| File | For |
|---|---|
| `vyrn.wasm` | the runtime |
| `program.mjs` | the program bundle, as bytes |
| `vyrn-edge.mjs` | the JavaScript above |
| `api/index.js` | a Vercel Edge Function that sends every request to the program |
| `vercel.json` | rewrites every path to that function |
| `worker.mjs` | a standard `fetch` handler for Cloudflare Workers, Deno and Bun |

```bash
vyrn build --target=wasm32-edge
```

```bash
cd build/edge && vercel deploy
```

A custom domain (for example `emvryx.app`) is attached in Vercel's project
settings, like for any other project; the routes are the program's own.

**How routing is kept.** On the edge the platform owns the socket. The VM
runs in *hosted* mode (`Vm::set_hosted`): `main:` runs as usual, so
`web.provide(...)` registers its providers, and `web.serve(...)` returns at
once instead of listening. Each request then arrives through
`Vm::handle_request(method, path, query, body, content_type)`, which uses
the same route matching, parameter conversion (path, query, JSON body into
the declared struct), providers and response rules as the TCP server.
`tests/web.rs` checks it without a socket, and the edge build of
`examples/api.vyrn` answered `GET`, `POST`, 404 and 201 identically to the
native server when driven by Node with web `Request` objects.

**What the host provides, and what is stubbed.** A WebAssembly module
with no imports has no operating system. What a program needs from one
is either given by the host through an export, or kept in memory, or
fails with a teaching error that a program can `catch`:

| Capability | On WebAssembly |
|---|---|
| Sockets (`web.serve` listening) | hosted mode: the platform delivers requests |
| Clock (`time.now`, `now`, `sleep`, `Clock`) | the host sets the time (`vyrn_set_time`, done by `vyrn-edge.mjs`); `sleep` moves a virtual clock forward at once instead of waiting |
| Secure random numbers (`vyrn.crypto`) | from a seed the host gives (`vyrn_seed`, from `crypto.getRandomValues`), stretched with SHA-256 |
| Files (`read_text`, `open`, `vyrn.fs`, CSV and JSON files) | an in-memory file system, emptied before each `vyrn_run` |
| Environment variables (`os.env`) | in memory, empty at the start of each run |
| Databases (`vyrn.db`) | SQLite, with databases in memory |
| Named time zones | the time-zone database is built in |
| Windows, sound, PNG images, threads, GPU | none; tensors run on the CPU path |
| Python and C bridges | not built for WebAssembly |

`src/vm/sys.rs` is the one place files, environment variables, time and
random bytes come from, so each has exactly two versions: the operating
system's, and the WebAssembly one.

## 3. The native tier (runs today)

Typed functions are compiled to machine code when a program loads, with
Cranelift (`src/native/`), on every platform `vyrn` runs on, with nothing
else installed. It works for `vyrn run`, the prompt, the language server's
checks and the executables `vyrn build` makes.

```vyrn
create fib(n: int) -> int:
    if n < 2: return n
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
end
```

**What compiles.** A top-level function or a struct method whose
parameters and result are `int`, `float`, `bool`, `str`, `[int]`,
`[float]`, or a struct whose fields are all `int`, `float` or `bool`, when
its body stays within those types:

- arithmetic, comparisons (chained too), `and`/`or`/`not`, `a if c else b`;
- `if`, `else if`, `else`, `loop`, `loop cond`, `each` over ranges,
  `range(...)` and lists, `stop`, `skip`, `return`;
- calls to other compiled functions and methods, recursion included, and
  `abs`, `min`, `max`, `sqrt`, `floor`, `ceil`, `int`, `float`, `exp`,
  `tanh` and the `vyrn.math` functions;
- **lists**: literals, `[]` typed by its context, `[x] * n`, `+`,
  comprehensions, `len`, indexing (negative too), item assignment,
  `append`, `copy`, `list(xs)`, `sum` of `[int]`, and lists as results;
- **structs**: constructors (by position or name), fields, field
  assignment, methods (not `mut self`, which writes back to the caller);
- **strings**: literals, interpolation with format specs (`"{x:.2f}"`),
  `+`, `*`, comparisons, `in`, `len`, indexing, `str()`, `int(text)`,
  `float(text)`, the common methods (`upper`, `strip`, `replace`,
  `startswith`, `find`, `count`, ...), and `print`.

Anything else (maps, sets, lists of strings or structs, objects, a
variable that changes type, `int ** n` with a non-literal `n`, whose type
depends on `n`'s sign) leaves the function to the interpreter, and a call
to an interpreted function keeps its caller interpreted too. A list or
struct argument is checked item by item when the call starts: a list of
`int` given where `[float]` is declared runs on the interpreter.

**How values are kept.** List items are read and written in place (the
layout of the VM's lists and values is measured at startup and checked;
if the check fails, items go through runtime calls). A struct is a stack
slot of one word per field, and every variable owns its own, which is
the interpreter's value semantics. Strings point at the VM's own
reference-counted text. Strings and lists made during a call live in an
arena the VM owns; at the end of each loop round the ones no variable
still holds are freed, so a loop that builds a million temporary strings
does not keep them. String methods, conversions, `print` and string
indexing run the VM's own code, so they cannot behave differently.

**Nothing changes but speed.** The interpreter calls the machine code
only when the arguments have exactly the declared types, and runs the
bytecode otherwise. Integer overflow, division by zero, `//` and `%`
rounding toward negative infinity, `/` giving a float, NaN comparisons,
`min`/`max` keeping the first of equal values, and the limit of 10,000
nested calls all behave as in the interpreter, and failures come back
as the same errors, naming the function and line. `tests/native.rs` runs
every program both ways and requires the same output and the same errors,
including 120 randomly generated functions on edge-case inputs such as
the largest and smallest integers.

| Benchmark (one core) | Interpreter | Native tier | CPython 3.13 | C (`clang -O2`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `fib(30)`, recursion | 0.141 s | 0.007 s | 0.069 s | 0.003 s |
| 5M-step integer loop | 0.206 s | 0.008 s | 0.203 s | 0.005 s |
| Mandelbrot 300×200, floats | 0.374 s | 0.010 s | 0.224 s | 0.008 s |
| Collatz up to 300,000 | 2.380 s | 0.134 s | 2.144 s | 0.039 s |
| Bubble sort, 3,000 `[int]` | 0.453 s | 0.014 s | 0.239 s | |
| Sieve of primes to 2M, `[int]` | 0.413 s | 0.042 s | 0.103 s | |
| Orbit, 1M steps of `Vec2` struct methods | 0.955 s | 0.048 s | 0.675 s | |
| FizzBuzz to 1M, strings | 0.181 s | 0.055 s | | |

The gap to C is mostly the overflow checks, which C does not make.
String-heavy code gains least, because each string operation still
allocates as the interpreter's does.

**Seeing it.** `VYRN_NATIVE=verbose vyrn run file.vyrn` lists each
function and why it was or was not compiled; `vyrn bytecode` marks
compiled functions; `VYRN_NATIVE=off` turns the tier off. The cargo feature
`native` (on by default, never on WebAssembly) builds it.

**How it works.** For each candidate the lowering walks the syntax tree
with the types of every local known, produces Cranelift IR, and drops
the function if it meets anything outside the subset; this repeats until
the remaining functions only call each other. Each compiled function also
gets an entry point taking its arguments as an array of 64-bit words.
Failures are written to a small state block (`src/vm/native_abi.rs`)
that the VM turns into the usual error values.

## 4. Design: the rest of the native backend

Section 3 covers numbers. The design below extends it to every type, with
LLVM as a release tier.

Goal: a statically linked Linux binary whose Vyrn code is machine code, so
the inference loop around the GPU work has no interpreter between
operations.

### 4.1 Pipeline

```text
source ─▶ syntax tree ─▶ checker (src/check.rs) ─▶ VIR ─▶ LLVM IR ─▶ object ─▶ static link
                         types, borrows, null      SSA, typed,   inkwell     + vyrn_rt.a (musl)
                         safety, exhaustiveness    explicit RC                + tensor runtime
```

1. **VIR** (Vyrn IR, `docs/architecture.md` section 2) is built from the
   checked tree: SSA form, a type on every value, reference-count
   increments and decrements made explicit (and then removed where the
   borrow checker proves them unnecessary), and `when` lowered to
   decision trees, which the exhaustiveness check makes total.
2. **Types decide representation.** What the checker knows statically
   becomes LLVM's own types; what it does not (`any`, unannotated code)
   becomes a 16-byte tagged value, the same layout the VM uses, handled by
   calls into the runtime library. Typed code pays nothing for dynamic
   code elsewhere.

   | Vyrn | LLVM |
   |---|---|
   | `int`, `i32`, `f32`, `float`, `bool` | `i64`, `i32`, `float`, `double`, `i1` |
   | `struct` (value type) | an LLVM struct, passed by value or pointer |
   | `object`, `[T]`, `{K: V}`, `str` | pointer to a reference-counted runtime object |
   | `T?` | `{ i1, T }`, or a nullable pointer for reference types |
   | `tensor` | pointer to the runtime's `DeviceTensor` |
   | `any` | `{ i64 tag, i64 payload }` with runtime helpers |

3. **Tensor operations stay library calls.** `@`, element-wise math,
   placement and `kernel` functions lower to calls into the same tensor runtime
   the VM uses (`vyrn_rt_matmul(a, b)`), which dispatches to the CPU
   reference, wgpu, or a CUDA backend. The GPU kernels are already native,
   and what the backend removes is the interpretation between them.
4. **`async`** keeps the stackful tasks of the VM: each task gets its own
   stack (mmap'd, guard page), and `await` is a stack switch in the
   runtime. This keeps "any function can await", which stackless state
   machines would not.
5. **Linking.** The object file is linked against `vyrn_rt.a`, the Rust
   runtime (tensors, tasks, HTTP, the scheduler), built for
   `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`, with `-static`. The result needs nothing
   on the machine: no interpreter, no libc, no Python.

### 4.2 What a typed function becomes

```vyrn
strict create dot(a: [f32], b: [f32]) -> f32:
    var acc: f32 = 0.0
    each i in 0 until len(a):
        acc += a[i] * b[i]
    end
    return acc
end
```

```llvm
define float @dot(ptr %a, ptr %b) {
entry:
  %n = call i64 @vyrn_rt_list_len(ptr %a)
  %nb = call i64 @vyrn_rt_list_len(ptr %b)
  %short = icmp ult i64 %nb, %n
  br i1 %short, label %oob, label %check          ; one bounds check, hoisted
check:
  %empty = icmp eq i64 %n, 0
  br i1 %empty, label %exit, label %setup
setup:
  %pa = call ptr @vyrn_rt_list_f32_data(ptr %a)
  %pb = call ptr @vyrn_rt_list_f32_data(ptr %b)
  br label %loop
loop:
  %i = phi i64 [ 0, %setup ], [ %i1, %loop ]
  %acc = phi float [ 0.0, %setup ], [ %acc1, %loop ]
  %xa = getelementptr float, ptr %pa, i64 %i
  %xb = getelementptr float, ptr %pb, i64 %i
  %va = load float, ptr %xa
  %vb = load float, ptr %xb
  %acc1 = call float @llvm.fmuladd.f32(float %va, float %vb, float %acc)
  %i1 = add i64 %i, 1
  %done = icmp eq i64 %i1, %n
  br i1 %done, label %exit, label %loop
exit:
  %result = phi float [ 0.0, %check ], [ %acc1, %loop ]
  ret float %result
oob:
  call void @vyrn_rt_fail_index(i64 %n, i64 %nb)
  unreachable
}
```

`a` and `b` are shared borrows (the default parameter mode), so the
compiled function takes no reference-count operations, and the loop is a
plain counted loop with one hoisted bounds check. (Checked: LLVM 18's `llc`
compiles this IR as written.)

**Floating-point order.** Summing floats in a different order can change
the last bits of the result, so ordinary compiled code keeps the source's
order exactly, as the VM does, and LLVM leaves this loop scalar. In
`kernel` function code, whose results may already differ in the last bits between
CPU and GPU, the backend marks arithmetic `reassoc contract`; with that,
`opt -O2` for AVX2 turns the same loop into 8-wide vector code (also
checked). The trade-off is visible in the source, as rule 4 asks.

### 4.3 Order of work

1. Done: numbers, lists of numbers, structs of numbers and strings
   (section 3), validated against the bytecode VM. Next: maps, lists of
   strings and structs, and `object`s.
2. VIR, so the Cranelift and LLVM tiers share one lowering.
3. LLVM codegen from the same VIR (through `inkwell`), for release builds:
   `vyrn build --target=linux-musl --release` links statically against
   `vyrn_rt.a`.
4. The WebAssembly backend from the same VIR, replacing the VM in edge
   builds, with the same stubs and imports as section 2.2.

title: Unreal Engine
text:
# Vyrn in Unreal Engine

**VyrnScripting** is an Unreal Engine 5 plugin that lets you write gameplay
in Vyrn. Put a **Vyrn Script** component on an actor, point it at a
`.vyrn` file, and the script runs with the actor. It can move it, spawn
things, trace lines, read keys and talk to Blueprints. Save the file while
the game is running and the change shows straight away.

```vyrn
# Content/Scripts/spinner.vyrn
use unreal (rotate)

create tick(dt: float):
    rotate(yaw = 90 * dt)      # a quarter turn every second
end
```

## How it fits together

```
 your .vyrn scripts              Content/Scripts/door.vyrn, unreal.vyrn
        │  host.call("move", ...)          ▲ begin_play / tick(dt) / end_play
        ▼                                  │
 vyrn.dll   (the Vyrn runtime, built from runtime/embed, C API in vyrn.h)
        │                                  ▲
        ▼                                  │
 VyrnScripting plugin (C++)   UVyrnScriptComponent: loads the script, calls it
        │                     each frame, answers its host calls
        ▼
 Unreal Engine: actors, the world, Blueprints, input
```

- **runtime/embed** builds `vyrn.dll` (`libvyrn.so` on Linux,
  `libvyrn.dylib` on Mac). This is all of Vyrn as a library with a small C
  API (`include/vyrn.h`). Any C or C++ program can use it, not only Unreal.
- **unreal/VyrnScripting** is the Unreal plugin. It is a C++ module that
  loads the library, and a component that runs scripts.
- **unreal/VyrnScripting/Scripts/unreal.vyrn** is Vyrn's side: `Vec3`,
  `Rotator`, and friendly functions such as `location()`, `move()`,
  `spawn_actor()` and `trace()`.

Values cross between Vyrn and Unreal as JSON. That makes it simple and
safe, and fast enough for gameplay logic: AI, doors, pickups, turrets,
game rules and UI flow. Keep heavy per-frame maths over thousands of
objects in C++ or Niagara, and call it from Vyrn through a host function
of your own (see [Your own host functions](#your-own-host-functions-c)).

## What you need

- **Unreal Engine 5** with a C++ toolchain. On Windows that is Visual
  Studio 2022 (or Build Tools) with the **Game development with C++**
  workload. This is the same setup as any Unreal C++ project.
- **Rust**, to build `vyrn.dll`. This is the same setup you used to build
  `vyrn`.
- A **C++ project**. A Blueprint-only project gets C++ by adding one class
  in the editor: **Tools > New C++ Class > None > Create Class**.

## Install (Windows, PowerShell)

Close the Unreal Editor, then run this from the Vyrn folder:

```powershell
cd $HOME\Vyrn
```

```powershell
.\unreal\install-plugin.ps1 -Project "C:\Users\you\Documents\Unreal Projects\MyShooter"
```

If PowerShell says running scripts is disabled, allow it for this window
only, then run the command above again:

```powershell
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process Bypass
```

The script:

1. builds `vyrn.dll` (`cargo build --release --manifest-path runtime\embed\Cargo.toml`),
2. copies the plugin, with the DLL inside, to `MyShooter\Plugins\VyrnScripting`,
3. copies `unreal.vyrn` and the examples to `MyShooter\Content\Scripts`
   (it never overwrites a script you already have).

Open the project. When Unreal says the **VyrnScripting** module is
missing or out of date and asks to rebuild it, choose **Yes**. Check
**Edit > Plugins**: *Vyrn Scripting* should be ticked. The Output Log
shows `LogVyrn: Vyrn 0.4.0 is ready`.

Release builds of Vyrn also come with ready-made plugin zips
(`VyrnScripting-<version>-Win64.zip`, Linux, Mac). Unzip one into your
project's `Plugins` folder to skip building the DLL. Then copy
`unreal.vyrn` into `Content\Scripts` yourself.

### Doing it by hand (or on Linux and Mac)

```bash
cargo build --release --manifest-path runtime/embed/Cargo.toml
```

Then:

- Copy `unreal/VyrnScripting` to `YourProject/Plugins/VyrnScripting`.
- Copy the library from `runtime/embed/target/release/` into
  `Plugins/VyrnScripting/Source/ThirdParty/Vyrn/<platform>/`:
  - **Win64:** `vyrn.dll` and `vyrn.dll.lib`. Also copy `vyrn.dll` to
    `Plugins/VyrnScripting/Binaries/Win64/`.
  - **Linux:** `libvyrn.so`.
  - **Mac:** `libvyrn.dylib`.
- Copy the `.vyrn` files from `unreal/VyrnScripting/Scripts` to
  `YourProject/Content/Scripts`.

## Your first script

1. Drag a **Cube** into the level.
2. With it selected, click **Add** in the Details panel and choose **Vyrn Script**.
3. Set **Script** to `spinner.vyrn`.
4. Press **Play**: the cube turns and bobs.
5. Open `Content/Scripts/spinner.vyrn` in VS Code (the Vyrn extension
   gives colours, errors and completion). Change `DEFAULT_SPEED` to `360`
   and save. The cube speeds up without stopping the game.

If a script has a mistake, the error goes to the Output Log and the screen
with its file, line and column. The script's `tick` pauses until you fix
the file and save.

## Writing scripts

The component calls these functions, if the script has them:

| Function | When |
|---|---|
| `begin_play()` | once, when the game starts (or the actor spawns) |
| `tick(dt: float)` | every frame; `dt` is the seconds since the last one |
| `end_play()` | once, when the actor is removed or the game stops |
| `reloaded()` | after a hot reload; without it, `begin_play()` runs again |

A script lives as long as its actor, so `const` objects keep values from
frame to frame. Each actor with a Vyrn Script component runs its own copy
of the script:

```vyrn
use unreal (Vec3, location, set_location)

object Bob:
    start: Vec3 = Vec3()
    age: float = 0.0
end

const BOB = Bob()

create begin_play():
    BOB.start = location()
end

create tick(dt: float):
    BOB.age += dt
    set_location(BOB.start + Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 30.0 * BOB.age.sin()))
end
```

`print(...)` writes to the Output Log under `LogVyrn`, with the actor's
name.

### What `unreal.vyrn` gives you

Import what you use, `use unreal (Vec3, location, move)`, or all of it
with `use unreal` and then write `unreal.location()`.

Unreal measures in centimetres, degrees and seconds. X is forward, Y is
right and Z is up.

**Types**

| Name | What |
|---|---|
| `Vec3(x, y, z)` | a position or direction; `+ - *`, unary `-`, `.length()`, `.normalized()`, `.dot(v)` |
| `Rotator(pitch, yaw, roll)` | which way something faces |
| `Hit` | what `trace` hit: `.actor`, `.point`, `.normal`, `.distance` |

**This actor**

| Function | What |
|---|---|
| `me()` | the actor's name |
| `location()` / `set_location(p, sweep = false)` | where it is / put it somewhere (gives false if `sweep` hit something) |
| `move(by, sweep = true)` | move by an offset, stopping at walls; false if blocked |
| `rotation()` / `set_rotation(r)` | which way it faces |
| `rotate(pitch = 0, yaw = 0, roll = 0)` | turn by some degrees |
| `forward()` / `right()` | the directions it faces |
| `get_var(name, default = none)` / `set_var(name, value)` | the component's **Variables** |

**The world**

| Function | What |
|---|---|
| `time()` | game seconds since the level started |
| `player()` | the player pawn's name, or none |
| `find(tag)` | names of actors with a tag (Details > Actor > Tags) |
| `location_of(actor)` / `distance_to(actor)` | where another actor is / how far |
| `spawn_actor(class_path, at, facing = Rotator())` | place an actor; gives its name, or none |
| `destroy(actor)` | remove an actor |
| `trace(start, finish)` | a line through the world: the first `Hit`, or none |
| `key_down(key)` | whether a key is held: `"W"`, `"SpaceBar"`, `"LeftMouseButton"`, `"Gamepad_FaceButton_Bottom"` |

**Messages**

| Function | What |
|---|---|
| `log(x)` / `warn(x)` / `error(x)` | to the Output Log |
| `screen(text, seconds = 2, color = "white")` | on the game screen (`"red"`, `"#ff8800"`, ...) |
| `event(name, data = none)` | fires the component's **On Script Event** in Blueprints |

For `spawn_actor`, get a Blueprint's class path by right-clicking it in
the Content Browser and choosing **Copy Reference**. That gives
`/Script/Engine.Blueprint'/Game/FPS/BP_Rocket.BP_Rocket'`. Use the part
in quotes and add `_C`: `"/Game/FPS/BP_Rocket.BP_Rocket_C"`. Engine
classes are written like `"/Script/Engine.PointLight"`.

Actors are referred to by name, the text that `find`, `player` and
`spawn_actor` give. Names stay valid until the actor is destroyed. `"self"`
means the script's own actor.

**Any property, any function** (Unreal's reflection: no C++ needed)

| Function | What |
|---|---|
| `get(actor, "Health")` | a variable of an actor or its Blueprint; `"Mesh.RelativeScale3D"` reaches a component's |
| `set(actor, "Health", 50)` | changes one |
| `call(actor, "OpenDoor", args...)` | runs any Blueprint-callable function or custom event; gives its return value (or a map of its outputs) |

Numbers, true/false, text, names, vectors (`{"x", "y", "z"}`), rotators
and actors come across as Vyrn values; anything else (an enum, a colour)
as Unreal's text for it, which `set` also accepts.

**Other actors**

| Function | What |
|---|---|
| `set_location_of(actor, p, sweep = false)`, `rotation_of(actor)`, `set_rotation_of(actor, r)` | moving and turning any actor |
| `class_of(actor)`, `tags_of(actor)` | what it is |
| `find_class("/Game/Enemies/BP_Enemy.BP_Enemy_C")` | every actor of a class |

**Enhanced Input**

| Function | What |
|---|---|
| `add_input_context("/Game/Input/IMC_Default.IMC_Default", priority = 0)` | turns on an Input Mapping Context (in `begin_play`) |
| `action("/Game/Input/IA_Move.IA_Move")` | an Input Action's value now: true/false, a number, or [x, y] for movement and looking |

**AI and animation**

| Function | What |
|---|---|
| `ai_move_to(actor, to, accept = 50)` | walks a pawn with an AI Controller there on the navigation mesh (add a Nav Mesh Bounds Volume); false if there is no way |
| `ai_stop(actor)`, `ai_moving(actor)` | stopping, and whether it is still walking |
| `play_montage(actor, "/Game/Anims/AM_Reload.AM_Reload", rate = 1)` | plays an Anim Montage on a Character; gives its length |
| `stop_montage(actor)` | stops it |

**Multiplayer**

In a multiplayer game every machine runs the script. Let the server decide
anything that matters (damage, scores, spawning): do it only where
`has_authority()` is true. Set Blueprint variables that are marked
*Replicated* with `set` on the server, and every player sees them.

| Function | What |
|---|---|
| `has_authority(actor = "self")` | whether this machine is in charge of the actor |
| `net_mode()` | `"standalone"`, `"client"`, `"listen_server"` or `"dedicated_server"` |
| `set_replicates(on = true, actor = "self")` | sends the actor and its movement to every player |

### The examples

| Script | What it shows |
|---|---|
| `spinner.vyrn` | the three event functions, Variables, state that lasts between frames |
| `door.vyrn` | reacting to the player's distance, easing, telling Blueprints with `event` |
| `turret.vyrn` | an FPS turret: turning towards the player, line-of-sight traces, spawning projectiles on a cooldown |
| `enemy.vyrn` | an enemy that chases the player on the navigation mesh, plays an attack montage, and hits by calling the player's Blueprint event, deciding only on the server |

## Vyrn and Blueprints

**Variables (editor to script):** the component's *Variables* map holds
per-actor settings. Add `speed` = `180` on one spinner and `30` on
another, and the same script reads them with `get_var("speed", 90)`.
Numbers and `true`/`false` arrive as numbers and booleans, and anything
else arrives as text. Scripts can write them with `set_var`, and
Blueprints can read the map.

**Events (script to Blueprint):** `event("door_opened")` or
`event("scored", {"points": 10})` fires **On Script Event (Name, Data
Json)** on the component. In the actor's Blueprint, select the component
and click **+** next to *On Script Event*, then switch on *Name* to play
a sound, update the HUD, and so on. To read the fields of *Data Json* in
Blueprints, turn on Unreal's **Json Blueprint Utilities** plugin and use
its **Load Json from String** and **Get Field** nodes.

**Calls (Blueprint to script):** the **Call Function** node runs any
script function, with the arguments as a JSON list:

```
Call Function   Name: "take_damage"   Args Json: [25, "explosion"]
  → Return Value: the result as JSON    Success: true / false
```

Next to it: **Has Function**, **Reload Script**, **Get Last Error** and
**Get Script Path**.

## Your own host functions (C++)

Any C++ function can be given to scripts. Register it on the component.
The arguments arrive as JSON values, and you return JSON text:

```cpp
#include "VyrnScriptComponent.h"

void AMyCharacter::BeginPlay()
{
    // Before Super::BeginPlay(), so the script sees it from the start.
    if (UVyrnScriptComponent* Script = FindComponentByClass<UVyrnScriptComponent>())
    {
        Script->RegisterHostFunction(TEXT("ammo"), [this](const TArray<TSharedPtr<FJsonValue>>&)
        {
            return FString::FromInt(Ammo);
        });
        Script->RegisterHostFunction(TEXT("give_ammo"), [this, Script](const TArray<TSharedPtr<FJsonValue>>& Args)
        {
            if (Args.Num() < 1 || Args[0]->Type != EJson::Number)
            {
                Script->Fail(TEXT("give_ammo needs a number"));
                return FString();
            }
            Ammo += static_cast<int32>(Args[0]->AsNumber());
            return FString();
        });
    }
    Super::BeginPlay();
}
```

In the script:

```vyrn
use vyrn.host

create tick(dt: float):
    if host.call("ammo") < 5: host.call("give_ammo", 30)
end
```

A host function with the same name as a built-in one replaces it. For
example, register your own `"spawn"` to take spawned actors from a pool.
Before writing one, check whether `get`, `set` and `call` already reach
what you need: they cover any Blueprint variable, function and event.

`host.available()` is true inside Unreal, so a script can tell whether it
is running in the game or under `vyrn run` and `vyrn test`.

## Testing scripts without Unreal

The game rules in a script are ordinary Vyrn, so put them in functions
that take plain values and test them with `vyrn test`. This is the same
as the Asteroids project, whose `Game.update` takes the controls as a map.
Keep the `unreal.*` calls in thin `tick` functions.

The repository tests the plugin's scripts this way too.
`runtime/embed/tests/unreal_test.c` runs `spinner.vyrn`, `door.vyrn` and
`turret.vyrn` against a fake Unreal written in C, through the same
`vyrn.dll` API.

## Packaging the game

Scripts are plain files, not Unreal assets, so tell Unreal to ship them:
**Project Settings > Packaging > Additional Non-Asset Directories To
Copy** → add `Scripts`. The plugin's build rules already copy `vyrn.dll`
next to the game.

Turn off **Hot Reload** on the components for release builds if you don't
want players changing scripts. It costs only one file check every half
second either way.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|
| "The following modules are missing or built with a different engine version: VyrnScripting" | Choose **Yes** to rebuild. If it fails, right-click the `.uproject` > **Generate Visual Studio project files**, open the `.sln`, and build *Development Editor*. The first error in the Output window says what's wrong. |
| `Could not load the Vyrn runtime library` in the Output Log | `vyrn.dll` isn't in `Plugins\VyrnScripting\Binaries\Win64`. Run `install-plugin.ps1` again with the editor closed. |
| `LNK1181: cannot open input file 'vyrn.dll.lib'` | The library wasn't copied into `Source\ThirdParty\Vyrn\Win64`. Run `install-plugin.ps1` again. |
| `` `host` is not defined `` | Scripts that call `host.call` directly need `use vyrn.host`. `unreal.vyrn` already has it. |
| `the host has no function ...` | A typo in a `host.call` name, or a C++ function registered after the script called it. |
| `cannot read .../Content/Scripts/x.vyrn` | Check **Script** on the component. It is relative to `Content/Scripts`. |
| Copying fails because `vyrn.dll` is in use | Close the Unreal Editor first. |

The plugin is written against Unreal Engine 5's standard APIs (actor
components, `UGameplayStatics`, the Json module). Those have stayed stable
across 5.x. If your engine version reports a compile error in the plugin,
the first error line names the file and the API to adjust.

## Limits, for now

- Scripts run on the game thread, one engine per component. Each
  component's script has its own globals.
- Values cross as JSON, so pass names and numbers, not object handles.
  Actors are referred to by name.
- Arrays, maps and structs other than vectors and rotators are read and
  written as Unreal's text form, not as Vyrn lists and maps.
- Calls from one machine to another (RPCs) are made in Blueprints:
  have a script `call` a Blueprint event marked *Run on Server*.

title: Principles
blurb: Why Vyrn is the way it is.
text:
# Vyrn's Principles

Vyrn aims to be as easy as Python while keeping the best idea from each
major language and leaving that language's worst problem behind. Combining
everything is how languages become hard (C++, Scala, Perl), so every feature
is checked against the five rules below before it is added. A proposal that
breaks a rule needs a written reason, in its pull request, for why the rule
should give way.

## The five rules

### 1. One obvious way

Each task has one way to do it. A new feature must *replace* a pattern,
not add a second option for it.

- Module paths use dots everywhere: `use vyrn.http`, `use python.numpy`,
  `use app.storage`. There is no `::`, and no second spelling.
- Errors use `fail`, `attempt` and `catch`. There are no exceptions plus result types
  plus error codes.
- Each keyword names what the line does: `each` item, `loop` while a
  condition holds, `when` a value is this, `using` a resource, `attempt`
  something and `always` clean up, make an `object`. Python's shape is
  kept, but Vyrn has its own words, and the parser explains the Vyrn word
  when a Python one is typed out of habit.
- Blocks end with `end`. Indentation is for people, `end` is for the parser,
  so a lost tab cannot change what a program does.
- One formatter (`vyrn fmt`) with no options, so style never needs arguing.

### 2. The five-minute test

A beginner can learn a new feature in five minutes, or the feature stays
behind an opt-in keyword that beginners never meet.

| Everyone sees | Only those who opt in see |
|---|---|
| `x = 1`, `create`, `if`, `each`, `print`, lists, maps, f-strings | `strict`, `kernel`, `mut`/`own`/`move`, `on gpu[0]`, `region`, `unsafe`, `extern` |

Type annotations are optional. Code without them runs as dynamically as
Python; adding them buys checking where they are written.

### 3. Errors teach

Every error says what went wrong, where, and how to fix it, as Rust and Elm
do. An error that only says what went wrong is a bug in the compiler.

```text
error: cannot assign to `limit`: it is declared with `let`
 --> prices.vyrn:3:5
  |
3 |     limit = 20
  |     ^^^^^
  = hint: declare it with `var limit` to change it
```

### 4. No surprises

- **No implicit conversions.** `"3" + 1` is an error, not `"31"` or `4`.
  The only widening is `int` to `float`, which loses nothing that matters.
- **No hidden costs.** Copies of large values, allocations in `kernel`
  code, device transfers and blocking calls are visible in the source:
  `x on gpu[0]`, `str(view)`, `await`.
- **No hidden state.** No global interpreter lock, no mutable default
  arguments shared between calls, no loop variable shared by every closure.

### 5. Editions

Mistakes in the language get fixed without breaking anyone's code. Each
project names its edition in `vyrn.toml` (`edition = "2026"`). A new edition
may change a default or remove a feature, and `vyrn fix` rewrites code from
one edition to the next. Modules of different editions work together in
one program, so the ecosystem never splits the way Python 2 and 3 did.

## Python's problems, and Vyrn's answers

| Python problem | Vyrn | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Slow | Bytecode interpreter today; native compilation of typed code; `kernel` code to SIMD and GPU | Interpreter done, native code planned |
| No real multi-core (the GIL) | Green threads for waiting work; `task.Pool` OS threads for heavy work, with values crossing threads only by `own` | Green threads done |
| Type errors at run time | Gradual types checked before running (`vyrn check`) | Done |
| `None` errors | `T?` must be checked (`if x != none`, `??`, `?.`) before it is used as a `T` | Done |
| pip, venv, conda, poetry | One tool: `vyrn new`, `vyrn add`, `vyrn fmt`, `vyrn test`, `vyrn build`; dependencies locked by hash | Done |
| Hard to ship | `vyrn build` makes one executable file | Done |
| Indentation changes meaning | Blocks end with `end` | Done |
| Late-binding closures in loops | Each loop iteration has its own variable | Done |
| Mutable default arguments | Defaults are evaluated at each call | Done |
| Python 2 to 3 | Editions | Designed |

## The best idea from each language

| From | Vyrn takes | And leaves behind |
|---|---|---|
| Python | Readable syntax, comprehensions, `with` (spelled `using`), f-strings, the library ecosystem (through `use python.x`) | Speed, packaging, the GIL |
| Rust | Memory safety without a garbage collector, `match` (spelled `when`), enums with data, cargo-style tooling, editions, teaching errors | Lifetime annotations: borrows stay inside one function |
| Go | One formatter, single-file deploys, easy concurrency, fast builds, URL imports | `if err != nil` on every line |
| TypeScript | Types you add gradually | A type system too clever to read |
| Kotlin and Swift | Null safety with `T?`, `?.` and `??` | Needing an IDE to write code |
| JavaScript | `async`/`await`, running in the browser (WebAssembly) | `==` coercion and implicit conversions |
| Elixir and Erlang | Pipelines `\|>`, supervised task groups | Unfamiliar syntax |
| Zig | Compile-time code, no hidden allocations in fast code | Manual memory management |
| Julia and NumPy | Math that reads like math, built-in tensors, `@` | Slow startup |
| C and C++ | Direct access to hardware libraries through `extern "c"` | Undefined behaviour outside `unsafe` |

## Checking a proposal

Before a feature is added, its proposal answers:

1. Which existing pattern does it replace? (Rule 1)
2. Can a beginner learn it in five minutes, and if not, which keyword hides
   it? (Rule 2)
3. What do its error messages say, and what fix do they suggest? (Rule 3)
4. What does it cost, and where is that cost visible in the source? (Rule 4)
5. If it changes behaviour, which edition does it belong to? (Rule 5)

# Vyrn Master Architecture: Tiered Compiler and Data-Oriented Runtime

Status: draft v0.1, code samples updated to grammar v0.4. Nothing described here is implemented yet. Numbers marked
"target" are design budgets, not measurements.

Companion documents: [`grammar.ebnf`](grammar.ebnf) defines the syntax used in
every code sample below.

## 0. Goals and how they are reconciled

| Goal | Mechanism | Where the cost goes |
|---|---|---|
| Compile speed of Go | A custom dev backend that emits machine code directly from the IR, with function-level incremental rebuilds | Dev builds run roughly 2-4x slower than release builds |
| Execution speed of C++/Rust | A release backend with whole-program monomorphization and LLVM optimization | Release builds take minutes on large programs |
| Memory safety without a GC | Ownership, function-local borrow checking, ARC for shared objects | References cannot be stored freely; some patterns need `shared` or handles |
| Readability of Python | Indentation syntax, optional types, no lifetime annotations | Untyped code pays for boxing and dynamic dispatch until it is annotated |

"No compromise" is achieved per build, not per binary: the same source gets fast
compiles in the dev tier and fast execution in the release tier. The two tiers
share one front end and one IR, so they cannot disagree about what a program
means.

## 1. Compiler pipeline

```
 source (.vyrn)
     |
     v
  Parse ---------> AST            per file, parallel, no cross-file dependency
     |
     v
  Resolve + Type -> HIR           names bound, types inferred inside function bodies
     |
     v
  Lower ---------> VIR            SSA; ownership, borrows and ARC made explicit
     |                            borrow check, layout selection, async lowering
     |
     +------------------+--------------------------+
     |                  |                          |
     v                  v                          v
  DEV BACKEND      RELEASE BACKEND            TENSOR BACKEND
  single pass      whole-program VIR opts     tensor regions of VIR
  x86-64, arm64,   then LLVM                  lowered to MLIR
  wasm             x86-64, arm64, wasm        PTX, SPIR-V, CPU SIMD
```

### 1.1 Rules that keep the front end fast

These are language rules, chosen because they bound compiler work.

1. **Signatures are the inference boundary.** Types are inferred inside a function
   body, never across functions. A function's public signature is exactly what is
   written (omitted types mean `any`). Changing a body can never force another
   module to be re-typechecked.
2. **Modules form a DAG.** Import cycles are an error. Each module compiles to an
   interface summary (signatures, layouts, inlinable bodies) that dependents read
   instead of the source.
3. **Borrow checking is function-local.** References are second class: they may be
   parameters, locals and return values tied to a parameter, but they are not
   stored in heap fields. No lifetime variables exist, so there is no
   inter-procedural lifetime solving.
4. **No textual inclusion, no macros that generate declarations at parse time.**
   Decorators run on typed HIR and may not add top-level names.
5. **The compiler is a query engine.** Every stage is a memoized function of its
   inputs keyed by content hash. An edit invalidates only the queries that read
   the changed data.

### 1.2 VIR

VIR is the single mid-level IR and the contract between front end and backends.

- SSA with block arguments.
- Ownership is explicit: `move`, `borrow`, `borrow_mut`, `retain`, `release`, `drop`
  are instructions. The borrow checker and ARC optimizer run here.
- Types are fully resolved. `any` is a concrete boxed, tagged representation, so
  dynamic code needs no special handling in the backends.
- Data layout is explicit. A loop over a struct-of-arrays collection appears as
  loads and stores on individual columns (see section 3).
- Tensor operations are first-class instructions (`tensor.matmul`, `tensor.slice`,
  `tensor.place`), carrying dtype, shape and device in their types.
- Async functions are already lowered to state machines.

## 2. Pillar 1: Tiered backends

### 2.1 Dev backend

Purpose: the edit-run loop. Target: under 50 ms from saving a file to running the
changed code in a 500k-line project, and a cold build throughput above 1M
lines/s on 16 cores.

- **Direct emission.** One pass over VIR emits machine code using pre-assembled
  instruction templates with holes for operands (the copy-and-patch technique).
  No LLVM, no instruction selection DAG, no register allocation beyond a linear
  scan within a block. Targets: x86-64, AArch64, Wasm.
- **No linker in the loop.** Code is written into a persistent image with an
  indirection table for calls. Rebuilding a function writes a new body and
  updates one table slot. A running process can accept the patch, which gives
  hot reload for game and web development.
- **Generics without monomorphization.** A generic function compiles once and
  receives a hidden witness table (size, alignment, method pointers). This is
  the largest single saving in compile time and code size.
- **Checks on.** Bounds, overflow, shape and device checks all trap with source
  locations. A cycle-leak detector and a task-deadlock detector run in this tier.
- **Tensor code is not compiled.** Tensor instructions call a prebuilt kernel
  library (section 4.4), so editing model code never invokes MLIR.

Optimizations kept in the dev tier are the cheap ones that change asymptotic
behaviour: ARC pair elimination, column-wise loop generation for SoA data, and
inlining of trivial accessors.

### 2.2 Release backend

Purpose: maximum steady-state speed. Compile time is unconstrained.

1. **Whole-program VIR optimization**
   - Monomorphize all generics; specialize `any`-typed call sites whose argument
     types are known.
   - Devirtualize trait and class method calls using the closed-world class
     hierarchy.
   - Ownership optimization: turn copies into moves, remove retain/release pairs,
     promote `shared` values that never escape a thread to non-atomic counts, and
     promote non-escaping heap objects to the stack.
   - Layout optimization: hot/cold field splitting driven by profile data.
   - Async: inline and fuse state machines, remove allocations for tasks whose
     lifetime is bounded by their parent scope.
2. **LLVM** for scalar optimization, vectorization and code generation, with
   `noalias` on every borrow (exclusive borrows make this sound, and it is the
   main reason well-typed Vyrn should match C++ with `restrict` everywhere).
3. **Profile-guided optimization** using counters collected from dev-tier runs.
4. **Tensor regions** go to the tensor backend (section 4).

### 2.3 Keeping the tiers honest

- One semantics document, one conformance suite, run against both backends on
  every change.
- Differential fuzzing: random VIR is executed by both backends and results are
  compared.
- A release build never changes observable behaviour except by removing traps
  that the optimizer proves cannot fire. Overflow and bounds checks stay on in
  release unless disabled per function with `@unchecked`.

### 2.4 The interpreter (implemented)

The REPL and `vyrn run` use a bytecode interpreter that compiles straight from
the syntax tree (`src/vm`), after the checks in `src/check.rs` (section 2.5).
It needs no type information beyond those checks, so it also runs
unannotated, Python-style code.

**Register machine, not stack machine.** Each frame owns up to 256 registers;
instructions name their operands directly. `total = total + x` is one `Add`
reading and writing registers in place, where a stack machine needs four
instructions. Fewer instructions means fewer trips through dispatch, which
dominates interpreter time. Lua 5 made the same move for the same reason.

| Decision | Reason |
|---|---|
| 4-byte instructions (`Op` is a `Copy` enum, size checked by a test) | Dense code, one load per dispatch |
| 16-byte values, reference counted, no tracing collector | Matches the language's ownership model: memory is released when the last reference goes away |
| Structs copied on write (`Rc::make_mut`) | Value semantics without copying on every assignment |
| Sliding register windows | A callee's parameters are the caller's argument registers; arguments are never copied, and `mut` parameters write back for free |
| Non-recursive dispatch loop | Deep Vyrn recursion cannot overflow the Rust stack; the limit is a clean `StackOverflow` error at 10,000 frames |
| Counted loops (`ForPrep`/`ForLoop`) | `each i in 0 until n` costs one instruction per iteration |
| `TakeIndex` for `each mut` | The element is moved out of the list and back, so struct elements change in place with no copy |
| Dedicated `MatMul`, `Place`, `PushDevice`/`PopDevice` | Tensor work is dispatched to a `TensorBackend` per device; the VM never does tensor math itself |
| Failures unwind through handler records | `fail`/`catch`/`always` and `defer` cost nothing until something fails |

**Tensor backends.** `ReferenceBackend` runs every tensor instruction on the
CPU and is installed for all devices by default, so GPU-targeted code runs
anywhere with placement rules still enforced. Built with `--features gpu`,
`vyrn run` installs `WgpuBackend` (Vulkan, Metal or DirectX 12 through
wgpu) for `gpu[...]` devices when a GPU is present, and falls back to the
CPU otherwise (`VYRN_GPU=off` forces the CPU). Matrix products, element-wise
arithmetic, maps and softmax are WGSL compute shaders; `f16`, `bf16`, `q8`
and `q4` weights are uploaded packed and decoded in the shader, and weight
matrices of 256 KB or more stay resident on the GPU until the program drops
them, so a 4-bit model takes 4-bit memory in VRAM. Activations are copied
back after each operation, reductions run on the CPU, and work under 4096
elements stays on the CPU. The shaders are checked against the reference
backend in every format (`cargo test --features gpu`, which also runs on a
software Vulkan driver such as lavapipe). Other backends implement the same
trait and are installed with `Vm::set_gpu_backend`.

**Closures and calls.** Variables that closures use live in shared cells,
so assignments are seen on both sides and nested functions can recurse;
loop variables are new in each iteration, so each closure keeps its own.
Keyword arguments are matched at compile time when the callee is known and
by a `CallKw` instruction at run time otherwise (closures, methods, values
passed around). `using` closes its resources in reverse order on every exit.

**Tensor storage.** Tensors store `f32`, `f16`, `bf16`, or block-quantized
`q8`/`q4` (llama.cpp's Q8_0/Q4_0 layout). Compute is `f32`; matrix products
convert quantized weights a row at a time, never expanding them. Every
tensor counts against its device's memory, and `set_memory_limit` makes a
device enforce a capacity, so running out of GPU memory is caught in
development.

**Tasks in the interpreter.** Tasks are stackful: a suspended task keeps
its registers and call frames, so any function can `await`. Calling an
`async` function starts a task at once and runs it until it first waits (as in
JavaScript); the caller gets a task handle. `await` takes a task, a
channel, or a tuple or list of tasks (`join(a, b)` builds one).
`sleep(seconds)` and `channel()` (with `send`, `close`, `len`) are
built in, and `async each x in ch` reads a channel until it is closed.
The scheduler is a single-threaded ready queue plus timers; when every
task waits on something that can never happen, the program stops with a
`Deadlock` error. A task that fails and is never awaited is reported as a
warning. When `main` returns, tasks still running are cancelled; hosts
that keep a program alive call `Vm::run_pending`.

**Standard library in the interpreter.** `use vyrn.web` (or `vyrn.http`)
brings in `web.serve(port, host, requests)` and `web.provide(name,
value)`. The server is part of the scheduler: `web.serve` suspends the
calling task, the scheduler accepts connections while tasks wait, and each
request runs its route as a task, so a handler that awaits does not hold
up other requests. Route parameters come from the path, then the query
string, then `body` (the request body, parsed as JSON when it is JSON),
then the providers. A string result is sent as text, `(status, body)`
sets the status, `none` is 204, anything else is JSON; failures become
JSON errors whose status follows the kind (`NotFound` 404, `BadRequest`
400, otherwise 500). `Clock(hz, frames)` is in the prelude: `tick()` waits
for the next frame and returns the fixed step, `running`, `frame`,
`elapsed` and `fps` report on it, and `stop()` ends the loop.

**Interpreter-only limitations.** `spawn` of a plain (non-`async`)
function call runs it immediately. `par for` runs sequentially. Tasks
share one OS thread, and the HTTP server speaks plain HTTP/1.1 with one
request per connection (no TLS or keep-alive).

**Measured performance** (release build, best of 7, 4-core cloud VM,
CPython 3.13 on the same programs, outputs cross-checked):

| Workload | Vyrn VM | CPython 3.13 | Relative |
|---|---|---|---|
| 30M-iteration integer loop | 1118 ms | 1859 ms | 1.66x faster |
| `fib(30)`: 1.6M calls | 168 ms | 100 ms | 1.7x slower |
| 1,000 entities x 1,000 frames | 184 ms | 152 ms | 1.2x slower |

The last round of speed work, judged by instruction counts under callgrind
(wall-clock time on a shared VM is too noisy to compare small changes):

- Small integer operands are part of the instruction (`AddI`, `SubI`, `LtI`,
  ...), so `n - 1`, `i += 1` and `n < 2` need no separate load.
- A call whose result goes to a fresh temporary puts the function there, and
  `return` moves its value out instead of copying it: fib went from 17 to 12
  instructions per call, and 29% less time.
- Register stores skip the destructor call when the old value is a scalar,
  and `//` and `%` on integers no longer go through the general arithmetic
  routine.

A separate inner loop for simple instructions, on a register slice borrowed
once, cut instructions by up to a third but made calls and field-heavy code
slower in wall-clock time (the doubled dispatch code costs more in branch
prediction and cache than it saves), so it was dropped. Next, in order of
expected gain:

1. NaN-boxed 8-byte values, so scalars copy and drop without branches.
2. Frames that do not touch reference counts on call and return.
3. Inline caches for field and method lookup.
4. Fused compare-and-branch instructions.

## 3. Pillar 2: Data-oriented memory model

### 3.1 Ownership

| Form | Meaning | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| `struct` value | Owned, stored inline, moved or copied | None |
| `x: T` parameter | Shared read-only borrow | None |
| `mut x: T` parameter | Exclusive borrow | None |
| `own x: T` parameter | Ownership moves to the callee | None |
| `object` / `shared T` | Reference counted | Count updates, mostly elided statically |
| `weak T` | Non-owning reference to a shared value | Checked upgrade |
| `ptr T` | Raw pointer, only in `unsafe` | None |

There is no tracing collector. Cycles among `object` instances must be broken with
`weak`; the dev tier reports cycles that leak.

**Regions.** A region is a bump allocator with a scope. Everything allocated
inside is freed in one step when the scope ends, and the borrow checker prevents
references from escaping it. The runtime opens a region automatically per HTTP
request and per game frame, so most short-lived allocations cost a pointer
increment and are never individually freed.

### 3.2 Layout is a property of the container

Developers declare *what* an entity is. The compiler decides *how* it is stored,
based on where it is stored.

| Declaration | Default layout |
|---|---|
| A single `struct` value | Fields reordered by alignment to remove padding |
| `[T]` or `[T; N]` where `T` is a struct | **Struct of arrays**: one contiguous, 64-byte-aligned column per field |
| `bool` column | Bitset |
| Nested struct field (e.g. `pos: vec3`) | Kept together as one column of `vec3`; splitting is opt-in |
| `object` instance | Heap object with header; never SoA |

Opt-outs are explicit: `@layout(aos)` for collections accessed mostly by random
whole-element lookup, `@layout(c)` to fix field order for FFI.

Consequences:

- **Element references are row handles.** `each mut e in world` binds `e` to
  (collection, index). `e.pos` compiles to an indexed load from the `pos` column.
  The loop reads and writes only the columns it mentions, so untouched fields
  never enter the cache.
- **Stable identity uses handles, not pointers.** `pool[T]` is a SoA collection
  with generational indices. A `Handle[T]` is 8 bytes, survives reallocation and
  detects use after removal.
- **Columns are tensors.** `world.pos` is a zero-copy `tensor[f32; N, 3]` view.
  The same bytes can be iterated by game code, passed to a `kernel` function, or
  uploaded to a GPU buffer without conversion.
- **Parallelism falls out of the layout.** `par each mut e in world` splits by
  index range. The borrow checker proves iterations touch disjoint rows.

### 3.3 Game entity example

```vyrn
const GRAVITY = vec3(0.0, -9.81, 0.0)

struct Entity:
    pos: vec3
    vel: vec3
    health: f32 = 100.0
    name: str
    alive: bool = true
end

strict create step(mut world: [Entity], dt: f32):
    each mut e in world:
        if not e.alive: skip
        e.vel += GRAVITY * dt
        e.pos += e.vel * dt
    end
end

create lowest_point(world: [Entity]) -> f32: return min(world.pos[:, 1])
```

What the compiler does with it:

- `[Entity]` is stored as five columns. `step` touches three of them (`pos`, `vel`,
  `alive`); `health` and `name` are never loaded.
- `alive` is a bitset, so the skip test processes 64 entities per word.
- The loop body has no aliasing (exclusive borrow) and no calls, so the release
  backend vectorizes it.
- `world.pos[:, 1]` is a strided view over the `pos` column. No copy is made.

No layout annotation appears in the source.

### 3.4 Object-oriented programming

OOP is supported, with defaults chosen so that it does not undo the layout model.

- `object` gives identity, encapsulation (`pub`), methods and reference semantics.
- Polymorphism is through `trait`. Calls on a concrete type are static. Calls
  through a trait-typed value use a vtable, and the release tier devirtualizes
  them when the set of implementers is known.
- **Single implementation inheritance for `object` only, no inheritance for
  `struct`.** Struct layouts stay flat and predictable; classes keep the
  modelling tool people expect. Grammar v0.4 spells it as in Python:
  `object Enemy(Actor):`.
- Guidance enforced by lints, not by the type system: classes for long-lived
  objects with identity (scenes, services, connections), structs in collections
  for anything that exists in the thousands.

## 4. Pillar 3: The ML / GPU bridge

### 4.1 Hybrid lowering

General code and tensor code start in the same IR and separate late.

```
 VIR function
   |
   |-- scalar / control-flow instructions ----> dev or release backend --> x86-64 / arm64 / wasm
   |
   `-- maximal runs of tensor.* instructions
           |
           v
        Tensor region (dataflow graph, shapes symbolic or concrete)
           |
           v
        MLIR: high-level tensor ops -> linalg -> loops / vector
           |
           +--> GPU dialect -> NVVM -> LLVM NVPTX -> PTX      (NVIDIA)
           +--> GPU dialect -> SPIR-V                         (Vulkan, WebGPU)
           `--> LLVM -> AVX-512 / NEON / SVE                  (CPU fallback)
```

- **Region formation** happens in VIR. Any `kernel` function is one region. In other
  functions, adjacent tensor instructions are grouped automatically. Scalar code
  between tensor operations stays on the CPU path and calls into the region.
- **What crosses the boundary** is a typed handle: (device, buffer, dtype, shape,
  strides). No serialization, no interpreter, no Python-style dispatch.
- **Graph-level optimization** runs before MLIR: operator fusion, constant
  folding of shapes, common subexpression elimination, in-place update when the
  borrow checker proves the input is dead, and memory planning (buffer reuse
  from liveness).
- **Custom tensor dialect.** Vyrn defines its own MLIR dialect for the high-level
  operations so that fusion and placement decisions are made with full type and
  ownership information, then lowers to upstream dialects.

The exact upstream MLIR pass pipeline changes between LLVM releases and must be
pinned and verified against the LLVM version adopted at implementation time.
Per-kernel performance tuning (tiling, scheduling, vendor-library substitution)
is an empirical workstream, not something this document can settle.

### 4.2 Devices in the type system

- A tensor type carries its device: `tensor[f16; V, D] on gpu[0]`.
- `on gpu[i]:` ... `end` sets the device for allocations and kernels in a
  block. The same keyword names a memory region: `on frame:` ... `end`.
- `x on gpu[1]` is an explicit transfer. Mixing devices in one operation without
  a transfer is a compile error in strict code and a trap in dynamic code, so
  hidden host-device copies cannot occur.
- Ownership applies to device memory exactly as to host memory. Dropping the last
  owner frees the device buffer deterministically; there is no finalizer queue.

### 4.3 Multi-GPU execution for a 14B-parameter model

Sizing: 14B parameters is about 28 GB at 16-bit, 14 GB at 8-bit and 7 GB at
4-bit, before activations and KV cache. The runtime therefore assumes weights
may not fit on one device.

- **Weights are memory-mapped.** A model file is a header plus aligned raw
  columns. Loading maps the file and transfers each shard to its device from
  pinned memory. Startup cost is I/O, not parsing.
- **Sharding is declared, not hand-coded.** `on gpu[0 to 3]` on a weight collection
  asks the planner to place layers across devices; the planner balances memory
  and minimizes the number of activation transfers.
- **Pipeline parallelism for inference.** Each device runs its contiguous slice
  of layers. Only the activation tensor crosses devices, once per boundary.
- **Data parallelism for training.** `par for` over devices runs replicas;
  gradients are reduced with a built-in all-reduce.
- **Automatic differentiation** is a transformation on tensor regions in VIR,
  performed before lowering, so the backward pass gets the same fusion and
  memory planning as the forward pass.
- **Async integration.** A kernel launch returns a future. Web handlers `await`
  inference without blocking a scheduler thread, and the runtime batches
  concurrent requests into one launch when shapes allow.

### 4.4 Tensor code in the dev tier

Compiling through MLIR is too slow for the edit-run loop, so the dev tier does
not do it.

- Each tensor instruction dispatches to a prebuilt kernel library shipped with
  the toolchain (one generic implementation per operation, per device).
- Fused, specialized kernels from previous release builds are cached on disk by
  hash of (region graph, dtypes, shapes, device) and reused by dev builds when
  present.
- Shape and device errors are still reported at compile time in strict code,
  because that checking happens in the front end.

### 4.5 Tensor example

```vyrn
kernel create attention(
    q: tensor[f16; B, H, T, D],
    k: tensor[f16; B, H, T, D],
    v: tensor[f16; B, H, T, D],
    mask: tensor[bool; T, T],
) -> tensor[f16; B, H, T, D]:
    let scores = (q @ k.mT) / sqrt(D)
    return softmax(where(mask, scores, -inf), axis = -1) @ v
end

strict create generate(model: Model on gpu[0 to 3], prompt: tensor[i32; B, T]) -> tensor[i32; B]:
    var h = model.embed[prompt]
    each layer in model.layers:
        on layer.device: h = layer.forward(h)
    end
    return argmax(h[:, -1] @ model.unembed, axis = -1) on cpu
end
```

What the compiler does with it:

- `attention` becomes one tensor region. The two matrix products, the mask and
  the softmax are fused where profitable and emitted as PTX. A mismatch between
  the shapes of `q`, `k` and `v` is a compile error.
- `model.embed[prompt]` is a gather, a native indexing form.
- `on layer.device:` moves `h` only when consecutive layers are on different
  devices.
- The final `on cpu` is the only host transfer, and it moves `B` integers.

## 5. Pillar 4: Concurrency and web

### 5.1 Tasks

- `async` function compiles to a stackless state machine. A suspended task is a small
  heap or region object, typically a few hundred bytes, so millions can exist.
- `spawn f()` starts a task and returns a handle. `await` suspends.
- Scheduler: M:N work stealing by default. Servers can select thread-per-core,
  where each core owns its tasks, sockets and region, and nothing is shared
  across cores without an explicit channel.
- I/O: io_uring on Linux, kqueue on macOS and BSD, IOCP on Windows, and the host
  event loop on Wasm.
- **Structured concurrency.** A task cannot outlive the scope that spawned it
  unless it is explicitly detached. Leaving a scope awaits or cancels its
  children. This is also what allows child tasks to borrow from the parent.
- Blocking calls made from async code are moved to a blocking pool
  automatically, so a slow FFI call cannot stall a scheduler thread.

### 5.2 Data-race freedom

Guaranteed at compile time, by the same rules as single-threaded code:

- A value moved into a task is no longer accessible to the spawner.
- Any number of tasks may hold read-only borrows, or one may hold a `mut` borrow.
- Whether a type may cross a task boundary is inferred from its fields. `shared T`
  uses atomic counts only when the compiler sees it cross threads.
- Shared mutable state requires a synchronization type (`Mutex[T]`, `Atomic[T]`,
  `Channel[T]`). The data lives inside the lock, so it cannot be reached without
  holding it.

### 5.3 Deadlocks

Deadlock freedom cannot be proven for arbitrary programs. The design removes the
common causes statically and detects the rest.

| Cause | Handling |
|---|---|
| Holding a lock across `await` | Compile error |
| Acquiring two locks in inconsistent order | `using a.lock(), b.lock():` acquires in a canonical order. Nested acquisition of two `Mutex` values requires declared lock levels, checked at compile time |
| Re-locking a held mutex | Compile error when visible in one function; dev-tier trap otherwise |
| Tasks waiting on each other through channels | Not prevented statically. The dev tier maintains a wait-for graph and reports the cycle with task backtraces |
| Forgotten task that never completes | Prevented by structured concurrency |

The claim made to users is therefore: no data races ever, no mutex deadlocks in
code that compiles, and channel deadlocks diagnosed in development.

### 5.4 Web routes

`route` declarations are compiled, not registered at run time.

- All routes in the program are merged into one static radix tree at compile
  time. Conflicting or unreachable routes are compile errors.
- Path and query parameters are parsed straight into their declared types.
- JSON encoders and decoders are generated per struct type at compile time. No
  reflection, no intermediate document tree.
- Each request runs in its own region. The response is written, then the region
  is released in one step.
- Provider parameters (database pools, configuration) are resolved at compile
  time; a missing provider is a compile error.

```vyrn
route GET "/users/{id}" (id: u64, db: Db) -> User fails NotFound:
    return await db.users.find(id)
end

route POST "/generate" (req: Prompt, model: Model) -> Completion:
    let tokens = await model.generate(req.tokens)
    return Completion(text = decode(tokens))
end
```

### 5.5 WebAssembly

- Both backends emit Wasm. The dev backend targets it directly for fast browser
  iteration.
- `export "wasm" create` and `extern "js"` generate the JavaScript glue and
  TypeScript declarations.
- `await` on a JavaScript promise suspends the task and resumes from the host
  event loop.
- Tensor regions lower to SPIR-V for WebGPU, with Wasm SIMD as the fallback.

## 6. Risks and open decisions

1. **Two backends doubles the code generation surface.** Mitigated by the shared
   VIR and differential testing, but it is the largest ongoing cost of this
   design.
2. **SoA by default is not always faster.** Random whole-element access is slower
   than with array-of-structs. The default needs validation on real workloads,
   and `@layout(aos)` must stay cheap to apply.
3. **Second-class references restrict some designs** (self-referential structures,
   iterators that store borrows). The escape hatches are handles, `shared`, and
   `unsafe`. This needs testing against real programs before it is frozen.
4. **Dev and release generics differ in mechanism** (witness tables versus
   monomorphization). Semantics are identical; performance characteristics are
   not, and performance bugs may only appear in one tier.
5. **Gradual typing boundary.** Typed code calling untyped code inserts run-time
   checks. Their cost and their error messages need a dedicated design.
6. **GPU portability.** PTX is NVIDIA-only. SPIR-V coverage for the full tensor
   operation set, and AMD and Apple targets, are unscheduled.
7. **Class inheritance** is limited to one base class (section 3.4); whether
   that is enough for real game and UI code needs validating.

### 2.5 Checks before code generation (implemented)

`src/check.rs` runs on the syntax tree before the interpreter compiles it,
and `vyrn check <file>` runs it alone. It reports only what it is sure of:
anything it cannot infer is `any`, so unannotated code behaves as in
Python and annotations buy static errors where they are written.

| Rule | Example it rejects |
|---|---|
| Annotated bindings, assignments, arguments, returns and fields match | `let n: int = "seven"`, `area(2, "3")` |
| A function with a return type returns on every path | `create sign(x: int) -> int` ending in an `if` with no `else` |
| Fields and methods exist on structs and classes declared in the file (base classes included) | `p.z` on a `Point` |
| Obvious operator mistakes between known scalars | `1 + "a"` |
| `let` is not reassigned, passed as `mut`, or changed through a struct field or `mut self` method | `let limit = 10` then `limit = 20` |
| `strict`/`kernel`: typed parameters, no `any`, variables declared with `let`/`var`, parameters read-only unless `mut` | `strict create scale(v, k: float)` |
| No use after `move`, including "may have been moved" across branches and loop iterations | `keep(move xs)` then `print(xs)` |
| A `mut` argument is the only use of that variable in the call | `swap(mut xs, mut xs)`, `add(mut xs, xs)` |
| An argument for a `mut` parameter says `mut` | `reset(xs)` where `reset(mut xs)` |
| The list an `each mut` loop changes is not used inside it | `each mut x in xs: x += len(xs)` |
| Changing a field of a plain `each` loop's struct copy, which is lost | `each e in es: e.hp = 10` |
| A `T?` is checked before it is used as a `T`: narrowed by `if x != none:`, an early `return`, `and`, `??`, `?.` or `if let` | `u.name` where `u: User?` |
| A `when` over an enum declared here, a `bool` or a `T?` handles every case or has `else:` | a `when` on `Shape` without `Shape.Empty` |
| Generic functions infer their type parameters at each call | `pair(1, "a")` for `create pair[T](a: T, b: T)` |
| C functions that pass or return pointers are called in `unsafe:` | `accel_add(h, x, n)` outside `unsafe:` |

The `each mut` rule is what makes the interpreter's in-place loop sound: the
loop moves each element out of the list while the body runs, so any other
use of the list inside could see the gap. What is not checked yet: generic
structs, trait conformance, borrows through aliases (`ys = xs` then a use of
`ys` inside `each mut x in xs`), and references stored in other values.

## 7. Build order

1. Front end to VIR, with the borrow checker, validated by an interpreter.
   *Done so far: lexer, parser, AST, the bytecode interpreter (section 2.4)
   and gradual type and borrow checks (section 2.5). VIR is next.*
2. Dev backend for x86-64. This is the first usable compiler.
3. SoA collections and regions.
4. Async runtime and `route`.
5. Tensor instructions with the prebuilt kernel library, single GPU.
6. Release backend through LLVM.
7. Tensor backend through MLIR, then multi-GPU planning.
8. Wasm targets, AArch64, hot reload.
